## P3/P4 GPU contact reaction readout checkpoint

Opt-in production GPU reaction capture now includes normal and tangential contact
loads. Automatic joint breaking with contacts remains explicitly rejected; the
contact-free break continuation path is unchanged.

- `contact_reaction_gpu.rs` and `contact_reactions.wgsl` retain device assembly of
  complete external COM wrenches and generalized velocity increments. Each contact
  contributes its normal force plus tangent impulse divided by the substep, with
  endpoint sign and the moment about that body's COM. The assembly starts from
  the separate frame external-wrench buffer, not the already loaded predictor
  force buffer. It feeds existing RNEA/reaction reconstruction without a substep
  host solve, allocation or readback.
- Acceleration reconstruction sums retained predictor and tangent increments,
  rather than subtracting rounded output/input rates. A sticky assembly fault
  (`33554432`) suppresses later publication and is handled by frame rollback.
- Normal-contact incidence retains immovable endpoints for reaction bookkeeping.
  Their predictor force remains the original external force, not the contact
  load. Finite checks still apply to that early-return path.
- Contact-response ownership excludes structurally immovable bodies, including
  fixed ancestors in articulations with movable descendants. Sharing a fixed
  support therefore does not merge independent dynamic contact islands or consume
  their combined per-island tangent capacity.
- Capture toggles and reaction substep-count recompilations preserve coordinate
  and FK-position residues when model stamps and published coordinates match.
  Coordinate edits and changed models still reset the residues.
- Contact scenes now explicitly reject non-equality finite joint-axis position
  bounds and speed caps. The old distance/cone guard did not cover scalar stops
  in otherwise unconstrained scenes. Exact equality locks remain allowed; this
  guard is not an implementation of unified joint/contact solving.

The new reaction lane has **six passing GPU tests** (five public runtime tests
and one private device-buffer fixture). `make test-primitives-contact-reactions-gpu`
ran the initial five; the subsequently added rollback test was run separately:

- Fixed-support reaction balances all normal/tangent contact forces, support
  gravity and COM moments at both horizontal gravity signs and one/four substeps.
  CPU/GPU reaction agreement is checked at `0.01`, contact-wrench reconstruction
  at `1e-4`, free-root residual at `1e-3` and position agreement at `3e-5 m`.
- Capture toggles and one/three/eight substeps produce exactly the same published
  poses and velocities as the capture-disabled world over 60 frames with tiny
  translation increments.
- Two four-pad bodies sharing a fixed-joint support fit separate four-contact
  islands, including after adding a movable child to the support articulation.
- Unsupported scalar bounds fail before state advancement; removing the bound
  allows contact stepping again.
- A true `BodyKind::Fixed` endpoint receives the complete contact COM wrench in
  reaction assembly while retaining zero predictor force.
- A capture-enabled warm pipeline rejects nonfinite input without advancing the
  scene or retaining contact/reaction samples. Recovery adds no model compilation
  and agrees with an unfaulted GPU twin within `1e-7 m`, `1e-6` spatial velocity and
  `1e-4` support wrench. This compares transient motion rather than assuming
  equilibrium after 30 ms; the initial equilibrium assertion failed.

The baseline new lane failed before implementation (capture rejected and fixed
support islands merged). Development exposed and corrected a WGSL reserved name
and two fixture errors: a support's initial pose disagreed with its fixed-joint
frame, and an explicitly fixed body was given a duplicate world-root joint.
The final fixtures retain finite sphere-box contact geometry and include separate
coverage of authored fixed joints and actual immovable body flags. Evidence is
`contact-reactions-before.log` and `contact-reactions-final.log` under
`benchmarks/primitives/contact-gpu-2026-09-28/`.

Regression validation passes **27 existing GPU tests**, for **33 unique GPU tests**
in this checkpoint: four normal-contact, eight contact-free runtime reaction,
nine contact-response and six public contact-runtime tests, plus the six above.
The response suite includes full holding, sliding, re-stick/reversal and breakaway

## P3/P4 contact-driven GPU break continuation checkpoint

Supported tree-contact scenes now evaluate GPU break thresholds from the assembled
normal/tangent reaction loads, including when public reaction capture is disabled.
This supersedes the contact-breaking guard recorded above. Mixed distance/cone/
finite-axis-bound contact solving, contact sleeping and nonzero restitution remain
unsupported; removing the break guard does not close those packages.

- `rigid_world_gpu.rs` retains the original compiled GPU pipeline and solver across
  topology-changing segments. A break rebuilds the model/collision permissions and
  continues the remaining substeps. Failure after detachment restores the original
  scene, solver, bindings and frame-start precision checkpoint; provisional break
  events and contact/reaction samples are not published. Successful frames release
  the retained original resources. Prepared bind-group diagnostics track the new
  compilation even when a break occurs at the final substep.
- `rigid_contact_precision_gpu.rs` and `contact_precision.wgsl` map unchanged joint
  coordinate residues through stable body/joint identities. Newly implicit Free
  roots take their translational residues from the old world-position buffer, plus
  the host seed's f32 rounding residual. Body-position residues carry across the
  rebuild. The transfer is device-side and runs only at detachment, with no host
  readback of the low-state buffers. Quaternion components remain uncompensated.
- Contact reaction assembly is prepared for either capture or active break limits.
  The existing device threshold/event reducer and stop flag still choose the safe
  boundary. Host topology work follows compact notification and boundary state
  readback; there is no CPU contact solve or per-substep host threshold decision.
- Detachment can enable previously excluded collisions. A live newly enabled
  sphere-sphere pair exposed EPA fault 8; it was not replaced with other geometry.
  The resident narrow phase now has an analytic sphere-sphere route with scaled
  distance, compensated depth and deterministic endpoint-symmetric coincident
  normals. Other general convex GJK/EPA paths are unchanged.
- A pre-existing nonzero shared status now suppresses new narrow-phase evaluation
  and retires scratch. This prevents halted post-break dispatches from producing
  additional collision faults. The former overflow regression expected scratch
  reconstruction while its sticky fault remained set; its stronger assertion now
  requires zero scratch until an explicit reset, followed by normal recovery.

## P1/P2/P4 shared GPU impulse-domain checkpoint

`ResidentCoupledConstraints` now minimizes one common quadratic over circular
friction disks, bilateral scalar impulses and nonnegative scalar impulses. This
is the optimization component for unified joint/contact response, **not yet a
mixed live-runtime solve**. The contact/distance and finite-axis-bound guards
remain in place. No sequential contact-then-joint correction is advertised as a
coupled solution.

- The existing retained disk shader accepts a device-owned block-kind buffer.
  Each block occupies two Gram rows; a scalar uses x with an exactly zero unused
  row/column, free y and disk metadata. The common Gram includes off-diagonal
  contact/joint response. Disk-only callers retain their existing interface and
  four owned buffers, one pipeline and one bind group; their unused kind binding
  aliases an existing read-only count buffer.
- Product projection uses circular disks, unrestricted scalar values, or the
  nonnegative half-line. Published-f32 physical KKT verification includes scalar
  stationarity/complementarity, and static-to-dynamic promotion occurs only after
  the entire mixed system converges. Scalar rows are not approximated with large
  disk radii. Scalar output regimes are 4 (bilateral) and 5 (nonnegative).
- A zero-response scalar row may already satisfy its KKT condition while an
  unrelated disk needs solving. The first GPU run exposed an unconditional fault
  in this case; the zero-operator branch now checks each scalar's actual residual.
  Incompatible scalar data and contradictory/unbounded test systems fail closed.
- Eight mixed GPU tests pass: analytic contact/bilateral and active/inactive
  nonnegative solutions at reciprocal scales; globally static friction despite
  an independently overloaded contact; independent f64 KKT/quadratic-objective reconstruction
  for 70 mixed islands, all block orders and scales from `1e-12` to `1e12`;
  sticky faults and retirement/recovery; zero-response domains; contradictory
  bilateral rows; constructor validation; and 64 device-encoded solves in one
  submission with changing domains/counts/status and no intermediate readback.
- All six existing Coulomb-disk GPU tests pass unchanged. The first failure log
  also contains a test-only Rust literal inference error (f64 upload to an f32
  buffer), corrected independently of the solver fix. Workspace all-target
  checking passes with the existing unused test-helper warnings.

## P1/P2/P4 shared island and articulated-row assembly checkpoint

The common optimizer now has a device-side articulated assembly/application path
for both contact disks and scalar joint rows. `ScalarConstraintRow` supplies
body endpoints, scalar domain, active flag and input velocity minus target;
`ScalarConstraintBuffers` supplies dense model-global generalized Jacobians.
This remains a **pipeline component**, not enabled mixed `RigidWorld` stepping.

- `ResidentContactIslands::with_scalar_rows` merges contact and scalar incidence.
  Scalar rows have explicit graph vertices, retaining joint-only islands with no
  contacts and boundary-only rows with no responsive articulation. Shared fixed
  boundaries do not join otherwise independent dynamic response groups. Stable
  packed order is original normal rows followed by scalar rows. Articulation CSR
  excludes the scalar graph vertices; an immovable-only island has empty CSR.
- `ResidentContactResponse::with_constraints` computes all contact/joint and
  joint/joint Gram blocks using the same articulated mass factorization, sends
  disk/bilateral/nonnegative blocks to the shared optimizer, and applies one
  combined generalized impulse. Contact world impulses and original-order scalar
  solutions are separate outputs. Active scalar Jacobians are checked for finite
  values and nonzero columns outside their endpoint articulations. Faulted outputs
  remain untrusted; a subsequent halted invocation retires all output scratch.
- `DistanceGpu::new_for_coupling` reuses the existing radial/cone/scalar-stop
  geometry and anchor Jacobian construction to produce device scalar rows. This
  path does not solve joints separately and does not add the predictor increment
  to the exported input velocity. The shared response adds it exactly once.
  Scalar stops now retain actual parent/child body metadata for connectivity.
  The original distance-only dispatch remains available and is not replaced.
- Five new assembled-response GPU tests pass. They cover analytic coupled disk/
  bilateral and active/inactive nonnegative response at reciprocal mass scales,
  cross-articulation load transfer, joint-only and immovable-only rows, fault

  rows with a nonzero predictor increment, and device-generated locked-cone rows

- `ScalarJointPublication` converts common scalar multipliers into the existing

position-stop rows before contact correction. `RuntimeContacts` prepares the row

response, publishes scalar force/torque samples, reconstructs contact reactions,

consume the shared result, including scalar-stop-only scenes with no distance or

dependencies, assembles one `ArticulatedResponse` Gram matrix and applies one
common increment before final drift. The final drift does not solve those scalar
stops again. Exact equality locks remain native. Contact-only and non-contact
distance stepping retain their previous solver paths. The active/sleeping runtime
hook follows the same ordering with selected-articulation rows and drift.

assembly/readout; `coupled_constraints.rs` implements a separate f64 block-coordinate

impulses. It checks domain feasibility, physical row residuals at `1e-9`, and the
common objective before publishing. Static-to-dynamic promotion follows the global
solve. The contact-only solver and specialised track tangential-force ownership
were not replaced. No new public world API, GPU kernel or dependency was added.

## Redundant common-response allocation checkpoint

The common CPU/GPU solver now has a secondary allocation stage: minimize the
Euclidean norm of the physical SI row impulses among feasible primary quadratic
minimizers. This fixes a mathematical ambiguity, not a missing velocity solve.
The convention uses the existing unit-direction linear/angular Jacobian rows;
it is not an arbitrary-row-rescaling invariant or a compliance model. Changing
units or mixing differently normalized row definitions changes this convention.
The primary objective, friction caps, mode-promotion rule and velocity KKT gates
are unchanged. Contact-only specialized solvers are not replaced.

`constraint_allocation.rs` implements the CPU oracle. The mixed GPU shader uses
existing retained scratch only: no new buffer, dispatch, submission or readback.
Twice-orthogonalized rows of `G` and `free` define the affine set preserving
`G * impulse` and `free dot impulse`. Strictly sliding disks and strictly inactive
unilateral rows are fixed on their primary optimal faces. Dykstra projection from
zero onto this affine set and the impulse domains chooses the minimum-norm point.
Full-rank physical problems retain their original solution. Scalar padding rows
do not count toward physical rank. Fixed inactive rows retain exact zero, rather
than acquiring small positive impulses that violate complementarity.
When an affine radial constraint is tangent to a disk, facial reduction fixes its
two coordinates; plain alternating projection would otherwise converge too slowly
even from a supplied exact primary optimum. The CPU analytic tangent regression
first failed and then passed this reduction. This is not yet a broad tangent or
near-singular primary-solver certification.

Rank cutoffs are relative `1e-12` CPU and `1e-6` GPU after row normalization.
The secondary affine/stationarity residual uses normalized impulses: `1e-11` CPU
and eight f32 epsilons GPU. An initial experimental `2e-7` GPU secondary criterion
stalled at `2.00e-7`–`3.64e-7` in analytic redundant cases; measuring each stored
basis norm corrected most of this, and the eight-epsilon rounding allowance is
explicit. This does not relax the existing `1e-7` physical GPU KKT gate or the
`2e-7` analytic impulse-comparison assertion. A failed secondary solve or failed
post-allocation physical check faults the frame instead of publishing it.

CPU optimizer and mixed-runtime tests pass. All ten current GPU component
tests pass, including sixty redundant scale/rotation/order fixtures, repeated
execution and a strictly inactive stop sharing a redundant bilateral/contact set.
GPU component tests exposed and guided corrections for non-unit f32 basis vectors
and exact inactive faces. All eight current mixed GPU runtime tests now pass.
The two formerly failing reaction/break gates remain enabled and are stronger:
cone parity covers both interior and capped contact impulses, with an analytic
interior torque oracle; break decisions and event counts cover both `0.898 N m`
(break) and `0.902 N m` (no break). The loaded stop test still checks all 300
frames against its unchanged momentum/reaction bounds. Six standalone disk GPU
regressions also pass. No primary KKT, trajectory, reaction or break assertion was
weakened.

## P3 prescribed-boundary inverse-dynamics input — runtime propagation still open

The explicit acceleration oracle is now implemented independently of runtime
motion authoring. `rnea::inverse_dynamics_wrenches_with_boundary_accelerations`
accepts a dense body array of instantaneous world COM linear and angular inertial
accelerations. Only kinematic entries may be nonzero; wrong lengths, nonfinite
values and nonkinematic nonzero entries are errors. The existing API retains its
zero-acceleration behavior, with an exact-output regression.

The spatial recursion converts an authored boundary derivative to its translated
fixed-origin representation using
`a.linear = a_com - alpha cross center - omega cross v_com - gravity` and
`a.angular = alpha`. Simply adding linear acceleration or angular acceleration
without the reference-point shift would give incorrect off-centre loads.
The input does not replace gravity, external COM loads, Coriolis terms, gyroscopic
loads or relative joint acceleration.

`ReactionWrenchBuffers::boundary_acceleration` supplies the same input directly
to the retained GPU inverse-dynamics kernel. It is initialized to zero, adds one
`32 * max(body_count, 1)` byte persistent buffer, and raises this kernel's storage
binding requirement from 27 to 28. No per-evaluation allocation, upload or readback
is added by dispatch. The shader validates selected-body inputs, clears their
articulation's outputs before validation, and reports nonfinite or nonkinematic
acceleration faults through the existing status buffer. A later valid dispatch
resets status and recovers. Existing live runtime callers leave this new input zero.

Analytic CPU/GPU tests in `reaction_boundary_acceleration.rs` combine translating
and rotating boundaries, COM offsets, full inertia, gravity, external loads and
nonzero hinge/ball rates and accelerations. Twelve fixtures cover weld/hinge/ball,
two rotations and origin/translated positions. Initial CPU and GPU gates pass;
GPU peak scaled wrench error is `4.1627122306952556e-5`, against `3e-4`.
Retained nonzero-input resource checks cover forty dispatches; invalid input,
retirement, reset, undersized buffers and zero-DOF readback are also tested.
The zero-DOF test helper initially failed to map an empty readback; it now returns
an empty vector without creating a staging buffer. No physical gate changed.

## P3 live prescribed motion — CPU integration checkpoint

The opt-in `RigidScene::set_kinematic_acceleration(body, Some(acceleration))`
now advances a kinematic body's world COM and world angular velocity through the
CPU Featherstone runtime. `Some(SpatialVector::ZERO)` requests constant-velocity
motion; `None` preserves the existing externally authored, held pose/velocity
contract. Fixed/dynamic bodies and nonfinite accelerations are rejected atomically.
The acceleration setting is retained by stable handle across fork/rebuild and
temporary disable; changing mobility away from kinematic or deleting the body
clears it. Setting changes currently rebuild the model, not a hot-path buffer edit.

The model stores one dense acceleration array and an opt-in body flag. CPU ABA
includes the COM-to-spatial acceleration shift. Drift advances the COM with the
constant-acceleration formula and rotates with a world-angular-velocity midpoint
exponential, then reconstructs the body origin from its local COM. Angular motion
with noncollinear velocity and acceleration is second-order approximate, not exact.
Predictor/redrift both start from the original substep state; redrift also restores
input boundary geometry before scalar-stop mass evaluation.

Contact-only and common constraint assembly add the prescribed boundary velocity
increment at **input geometry**, including propagation through dynamic tree
descendants. Contact moving/static mode still uses the original input slip, not
the accelerated predicted slip. Distance/cone rows consume the same boundary
increment; scalar generalized-coordinate rows do not double-count it. Runtime
reaction recovery receives the explicit acceleration array. Initially stationary,
accelerating boundaries wake dependent sleepers. Disabled boundaries do not wake
dependents merely because their retained acceleration setting is nonzero.

## P3 live prescribed motion — GPU resident integration

The Featherstone shader now consumes the model's packed world COM/angular
acceleration buffer in its forward recursion and advances driven poses/velocities
during final FK. Prediction and drift-only dispatches seed from the original input
state, so repeated redrift does not advance boundaries twice. Offset-COM translation
uses the existing compensated position machinery when it is enabled. The midpoint
angular update follows the CPU contract rather than inferring acceleration from
rounded velocity differences.

Construction-time metadata records each body's nearest driven ancestor, stopping
at held/fixed boundaries. Contact response reuses a metadata word for that ancestor;
distance/cone endpoints reuse padding. Their free-velocity terms include the
prescribed acceleration at the original contact/anchor point. Contact classification
still consumes original input slip. Scalar generalized-coordinate bounds do not
receive a second boundary increment. GPU reaction reconstruction binds the same
model acceleration buffer, including after break-driven topology rebuilds.

This adds one storage binding to each affected shader: Featherstone 42→43,
contact response 30→31 and distance/cone response 21→22. Contact response's minimum
device storage-binding limit is updated accordingly. There is no new per-substep
dispatch, allocation or readback for motion/bias publication. Acceleration edits
still rebuild the model. GPU entry validation rejects nonzero values that overflow,
underflow or become subnormal in f32. Low-level GPU solver construction also rejects
driven bodies absent from an articulation; the runtime already compiles implicit
roots for isolated bodies. Membership validation is linear and constructor-only.

## Runtime translation precision — zero-coordinate and non-contact paths

Featherstone compensation now accepts states with bodies but no generalized
coordinates. Such states are identified by their pose buffers rather than by an
absent coordinate buffer; their coordinate-residue binding uses a four-byte dummy.
Duplicate pose-buffer registrations still fail atomically. Position residues are
copied through prediction/redrift even when there are no coordinate values to copy.

The runtime precision lifecycle is shared by contact and non-contact execution.
Both retain low coordinate/translation state across host frame publication,
same-model diagnostic rebuilds, and break detachment. Frame checkpoints participate
in ordinary failure recovery and whole-frame restoration after a detached segment
fails. Standalone distance/cone response now receives the retained coordinate
residues, matching the contact-coupled path. Explicit coordinate/pose edits reset
residues. Empty detachment transfer tables do not create a zero-sized shader table.

## Runtime mutation precision — identity-aware remapping

Ordinary model rebuilds now remap retained GPU coordinate/position residues by
stable body handle and insertion identity. Surviving, unchanged poses retain their
translation residues despite dense-index compaction. Matching joint owners, frames,
axis, reversal and coordinate values retain generalized-coordinate residues.
New implicit Free coordinates can inherit the old body's world translation residue
plus the host-to-f32 coordinate rounding term, including a changed COM frame.
New bodies, edited poses and incompatible coordinate bases do not inherit stale
residues. Contact/non-contact pipeline transitions use the same transfer lifecycle.

`RigidScene::body_identity_stamp` and `joint_identity_stamp` identify insertion,
not configuration. Edits and forks retain existing identities; independently
inserted objects do not share identities even if their numeric handles coincide.
This distinction also covers divergent forks, whose copied handle allocators can
subsequently issue equal handle numbers for different objects. Removal clears the
identity maps, including incident joints removed with a body. Failed edits retain
the previous identities.

Same-model pose edits now reset only affected precision state rather than clearing
all bodies. Their retained values are copied through checkpoint buffers, with
contiguous copy ranges and no new shader pipeline or GPU storage allocation for
that edit path. The edited input becomes the rollback baseline before stepping;
unrelated accumulated motion must survive a failed edited frame and retry. Cached
layout/identity metadata now belongs to `RuntimePrecision`, not the outer compiled
runtime. Rebuild transfer shaders remain under GPU validation scopes.

## P4/P5 restitution — measured runtime gap and coupled impact reference

The ordinary CPU rigid runtime does not consume contact restitution in
`penalty_contact::eval_contacts`; its normal response remains spring force plus
compression damping. The GPU runtime explicitly rejects nonzero restitution in
`rigid_world_gpu::validate`. Removing that GPU guard would not establish parity
with a correct physical response.

Added `runtime_restitution.rs` and `make test-primitives-restitution-cpu` as a
pending live acceptance gate. The fixture uses a one-kilogram sphere approaching
a fixed slab at one metre/second, zero gravity/friction/damping, stiffness 1e4,
16 substeps, and frame steps 1/60, 1/120 and 1/240. At each step size all three
authored coefficients (0, 0.5, 1) produce the same rebound speed:

| Frame step | Measured rebound for all three coefficients |
| --- | --- |
| 1/60 | 1.0003597564857172 m/s |
| 1/120 | 0.9999527497640442 m/s |
| 1/240 | 1.0000290343338758 m/s |

The dedicated target **fails** its 0.02 m/s coefficient-response gate. The test
is explicitly ignored in the default suite while integration is pending; the
dedicated target runs it with `--ignored`. It is not included in passing counts.
First-failure evidence is retained in
`benchmarks/primitives/restitution-oracle-2026-09-28/runtime-first.log`.

Added `impact_constraints.rs`, a standalone dense CPU reference, and
`make test-primitives-impact-oracle`. It solves three rows per contact (normal
and two tangents) together with bilateral/nonnegative scalar rows. The normal
residual is Newton's target-shifted relative velocity. Tangential disk capacity
uses the known predictor normal impulse plus the solved additional normal
impulse. The normal complementarity equation does not differentiate the friction
radius, avoiding associated-cone dilatancy. Static-to-dynamic promotion waits for
the common response to converge. Inputs receive finite/dimension/coefficient and
scaled positive-semidefinite checks; infeasible or nonconverged solves fail closed.

The reference has **15 passing tests**, including 60 normal mass/speed/coefficient

## P4/P5 impact energy — midpoint-friction reference and coupled contact blocks

Extended the impact reference with `solve_midpoint`, retaining `solve` as the
post-impact-friction comparison. The midpoint variant uses the average of pre-
and post-impulse tangential velocities. This is the impact-law construction
described by Acary and Collins-Craft; their paper also distinguishes zero average
slip from zero final slip. No complete Moreau–Jean time integrator is implemented
here. [Primary paper, sections 2.4 and 3](https://jtcam.episciences.org/15960/pdf).

In the implementation's unscaled row equations, tangent free velocities are
doubled while the normal restitution target is unchanged. The common Gram matrix
therefore stays symmetric. Friction regime and zero-slip diagnostics use half
the tangent residual, recovering the actual average velocity. Contact rows must
have current approaching or stationary normal velocities; stale onset speeds
and separating contacts are rejected by this entry point. Runtime active-set
selection is still outside the reference.

The earlier oblique counterexample is retained. Its post-impact-friction solution
still adds approximately 0.24913 energy units. The midpoint solution instead
has impulse `[2,0,0]`, outgoing relative velocity `[1,.8,0]`, and zero energy
change within the test tolerance. The normal coefficient is not reduced to obtain
this result. A separate capture test demonstrates final tangent velocity -0.2
from incoming +0.2 when average slip vanishes; `Solution.sticking` must not be
published as final resting contact without interpreting the selected law.

The first 540-case sweep exposed a real solver failure at mass 1e-6, normal/tangent
coupling .8, dynamic friction 2, restitution 0 and input tangent speed -3. The
previous split normal-then-tangent iteration did not converge. Replaced that
local iteration with a complete three-row contact block: eliminate the tangent
disk for a trial normal impulse, bracket the complementary normal root, then
bisect it. All outer joint/contact rows still share the common response and
global residual/mode-promotion checks. Invalid roots and nonfinite local response
fail explicitly; no tolerances or sweep cases were removed.

Evidence under `benchmarks/primitives/midpoint-impact-2026-09-28/`:

- `oracle-first.log`: 19 passing tests and the preserved high-friction failure.
- `oracle-block.log`: 20 passing tests after the three-row block fix, including
  all 540 combinations of three masses (1e-6, 1, 1e6), four positive-definite
  normal/tangent couplings, three friction coefficients, three restitution
  coefficients and five tangential velocities. Each checks total relative work,
  tangential work, normal rebound inequality and the circular Coulomb cap.
- The mixed-contact test checks individual normal/tangent work and shared
  bilateral/nonnegative joint response. Normal bounce tests retain authored
  restitution and two-body momentum over masses 1e-9 through 1e9.
- `oracle-final.log`: all 21 impact tests passed after adding the explicit
  stale-speed/separating-contact validation gate.
- `solver-lib.log`: 116 library tests passed, including those 21 impact tests;
  three timing benchmarks remain ignored. `check-all.log`: workspace all-target
  check passed with the existing unused `body_poses` helper warnings. No GPU
  execution was performed for this reference-only change.

For these approaching contacts, the normal complementarity relation gives normal
work `0.5 * (1-e) * incoming_normal_velocity * normal_impulse <= 0` on an active
normal row. The tangent impulse opposes its average velocity, so its relative
work is also nonpositive. These are instantaneous frozen-response checks, not a
proof for the existing spring predictor, changing geometry or a whole runtime
step. Scalar constraints and moving boundaries require their own work accounting.

The next integration boundary remains live contact activation/episode handling,
penalty spring/impact energy coexistence, assembly/readout, redundant allocation,
and the GPU-resident path. In particular, applying an instantaneous bounce while
leaving the same stored penalty energy to act afterward would double-count
restitution. No CPU/GPU runtime restitution gate is claimed passed here, and
the nonzero-restitution GPU rejection remains in place.

## P4/P5 articulated impact assembly — transactional CPU state response

Added `rigid_impulse::apply_impact` in `rigid_impulse/impact.rs`. It accepts a
supplied contact active set and bilateral/nonnegative scalar COM-wrench rows,
assembles their shared `J M^-1 J^T` response using the actual model and state,
solves midpoint-friction impacts, and applies the resulting generalized velocity
increments. Body velocities are reconstructed through the articulation, not
changed independently. The caller's state is replaced only after the complete
solve and finite-result checks; poses and persistent applied forces are retained.

This is an instantaneous articulated stage. It is **not yet called by
`RigidWorld::step`**. It does not detect contacts, choose an impact active set,
track episodes, integrate positions, update stored penalty energy, publish runtime
reaction/break samples or execute on the GPU. Its dense reference allocation is
not the required production GPU capacity/performance implementation. The API
remains provisional alongside the other primitives signatures.

Contact rows include offset-COM moment arms, both endpoint wrenches, physical
relative point velocity and world-space tangential surface velocity. Immovable
endpoints contribute prescribed velocity but no inverse-mass response. Scalar
rows share the same solve, allowing joint constraints to react simultaneously.
The result retains flat solver impulses, world contact impulses on the second
endpoint, relative impulse work, and prescribed-boundary work by block.

Boundary energy uses projected physical body momentum, not just reduced joint
rates. For a dynamic descendant of a moving kinematic ancestor, body velocity
contains inherited motion absent from relative joint rates. Using `J * qdot`
alone to partition work would give the wrong kinetic-energy change. The stage
computes `M^-1 * J_body^T * body_momentum` before projecting row energy rates.
Independent physical body-energy measurements verify the returned identity
`kinetic_energy_change = sum(relative_work + boundary_work)`.

Added `make test-primitives-articulated-impact-cpu` and `articulated_impact.rs`.
Coverage includes normal rebound at coefficients 0, .5 and 1 with mass ratios and
endpoint exchange; off-center impacts with COM offsets, rotated off-diagonal
inertia and large translations; fixed-tree momentum transfer; a world hinge's
pivot inertia; a moving support; inherited kinematic velocity; simultaneous
manifold contacts; coupled bilateral/nonnegative rows; circular impact friction,
frame covariance and energy; surface work; and atomic failure after assembly.

The moving-support fixture deliberately gains three units of dynamic-body kinetic
energy while losing three units of relative impact energy and receiving six units
of boundary work. The conveyor fixture gains .5 units, with -2.5 relative work
and +3 surface work. Normal surface-belt velocity is ignored consistently with
the existing tangential conveyor contract. These are measured boundary-work
transfers, not unexplained energy creation.

Evidence is under `benchmarks/primitives/articulated-impact-2026-09-28/`.
`first.log` retains a fixture construction failure: the initial proposed inertia
was positive definite but violated physical principal-moment triangle bounds.
The fixture tensor was corrected to a valid off-diagonal tensor, with expected
impulses still calculated from that tensor independently. `second.log` and
`final.log` contain the initial ten passing articulated tests. Runtime automatic
restitution and the complete primitives goal remain unfinished.

- `solver-lib.log`: **116 library tests passed**, three timing benchmarks ignored.

- `check-all.log`: workspace all-target check passed, retaining the pre-existing

- `runtime-still-pending.log`: the automatic `RigidWorld` restitution gate was

- Canonical branch remains `develop`; no commit or dependency/environment change.

## P4/P5 live CPU restitution — episode lifecycle and manifold correction

`rigid_impact.rs` now connects the articulated impact stage to ordinary and
sleep-selected `RigidWorld` stepping. Contact onset is identified by sorted stable
collider handles, collider stamps/authored poses, parent structure/state-edit
stamps and a canonical normal. Separation removes the episode; material, collider
and explicit body-state edits invalidate it. Endpoint ordering is canonicalized.
The cache is published only after successful scene commit and is included in the
whole-frame break checkpoint. This supersedes the earlier checkpoint's statement
that the impact stage is not called by `RigidWorld::step`.

On a new approaching contact, the onset penalty depth is temporarily suppressed
before force prediction. The shared midpoint impact response then uses the
predicted velocity, contact rows and selected joint/bound rows. Joint scalar rows
can now carry a direct generalized-DOF coefficient. Impacts select connected
dynamic groups, not every contact sharing a fixed ground. Contact impulse/force
readout and joint reaction samples include the physical impulse; friction regime
is classified from actual final point slip rather than midpoint-law stationarity.
Zero average slip can be a reversal, not a stationary final contact.

An initial persistent penetration-offset implementation passed rebound but failed
the existing loaded support-height gate: the resting height was approximately
`.4966603` instead of `.5 - 9.81/1e5`. That approach was removed. The current hook
uses a one-time mass-weighted linearized normal/joint position correction at onset,
integrates its pseudo rates only for impacted articulations, restores physical
rates, and redrifts the physical substep. It does not permanently alter spring rest
depth or advance prescribed boundaries twice. Original geometric penetration is
restored in contact force readouts.

The full library regression exposed a six-point near-dependent heightfield
manifold: first a velocity solve failure at tick 92, then a position solve failure
at tick 93 after the contact-only repair. The exact first velocity matrix and
domains are preserved in `bounds-matrix.log`; temporary instrumentation is removed.
The dense reference now has a bounded sticking active-set fallback covering
contact and nonnegative blocks plus mandatory bilateral rows. Each candidate is
checked against **every original row**, including inactive normal inequalities,
bilateral equalities, nonnegative impulses and friction disks at the original
`1e-10` relative residual tolerance. No rows or acceptance checks are discarded.
Near-parallel contact, scalar/bilateral and infeasible-candidate tests exercise it.
The previously failing retained-versus-rebuilt bounds test now passes all 600
steps, including geometry replacement, pose edits, sleeping, wake and failure.

This remains a provisional CPU implementation. The enumerated fallback is bounded
to eight switchable blocks and covers sticking candidates, not general sliding
active sets or canonical redundant-impulse allocation. Larger systems retain the
iterative fail-closed path. Position correction is linearized once; general deep
overlap, refreshed nonlinear manifolds, complete impact-active-set closure,
coupled compliant energy, broad floating-body momentum certification and the
production GPU implementation remain open. The fixed onset speed threshold and
normal-based episode matching also need wider scale/manifold acceptance.

## P4/P5 GPU midpoint impact solver — resident component checkpoint

Added `impact_constraints_gpu.rs`, `shaders/impact_constraints.wgsl` and
`make test-primitives-impact-gpu`. `ResidentImpactConstraints` consumes retained
device Gram matrices, free row velocities, block metadata, block counts and island
count. Each contact occupies three rows: normal plus two tangents. Bilateral and
nonnegative scalar blocks occupy one row with two required zero padding rows.
This differs from the existing two-row tangential disk solver: normal impact
impulses are unknown and determine the friction radii within the same solve.

The GPU law matches the CPU midpoint reference: normal Newton restitution and
Coulomb friction against average pre/post-impact tangent velocity. Contact input
requires current approaching/stationary normal speeds, not stale episode speeds.
The component has no predictor normal-offset impulse. Scalar rows share the
response, and static-to-dynamic promotion occurs only after common convergence.
Outputs distinguish final physical velocity from midpoint-law sticking.

Each island uses block iteration with a coupled three-row local contact solve.
For a trial normal impulse, the shader solves the tangent disk and brackets the
normal complementarity root. The tangent inverse uses scaled spectral directions,
including compatible singular response, without adding a physical regularizer.
Residual evaluation consumes the rounded physical impulses with compensated row
products. A final physical KKT check governs success; exhausting iterations is a
sticky fault, not an approximate-success return. This checkpoint has no GPU
near-dependent active-set fallback or canonical redundant-impact allocation.

Constructor checks reject invalid/overflowing capacities, storage-buffer sizes
and invalid tolerances before allocation. Device validation covers finite data,
material ordering, incoming-speed consistency, domain tags and scalar padding,
matrix symmetry/PSD within f32 validation tolerances and device-owned counts.
Fault bits occupy 25–28. Caller-owned status is sticky, including externally set
halt bits; all results must be ignored while status is nonzero. Old solution slots
are cleared each dispatch. The solve retains four buffers, one group and one
pipeline; `encode` performs no buffer allocation or host readback. Test readbacks
occur after submitted dispatch sequences, not inside the solver.

GPU evidence is under `benchmarks/primitives/impact-gpu-2026-09-28/`:

- `first.log`: preserved shader-validation failure because a helper named `read`
  shadowed WGSL's storage-access enumerant. Helpers now use `sread`/`swrite`.
- `second.log`: the initial three GPU tests passed, including 540 oblique cases.
- `expanded.log`: preserved singular-tangent failure in the determinant-based
  local inverse. The spectral disk solve and exclusion of failure sentinels from
  norm evaluation repaired both sliding and interior singular cases.
- `spectral-disk.log`: five GPU tests passed after that repair.
- `final-expanded.log`: seven GPU tests passed, adding tangent-basis covariance,
  zero-normal capacity, constructor/material/domain validation and count changes.
- `final-regression.log`: **8 impact GPU tests passed**, adding iteration-budget
  exhaustion, retained recovery and external-halt publication checks; **6 existing
  disk GPU tests** and **10 mixed-constraint GPU tests** also passed. Total: **24
  distinct GPU tests** for this checkpoint, not full runtime acceptance.
- `cpu-check.log`: **24 CPU impact-reference, 12 articulated-impact and 10 live
  restitution tests passed**; workspace all-target check passed with only the
  existing unused `body_poses` test-helper warnings. `format.log` records scoped
  Rust formatting verification; `git diff --check` passed.

The tests independently evaluate f64 KKT residuals from published f32 impulses,
compare physical response against the CPU midpoint oracle and measure impulse
work. Coverage includes the 540-case mass/friction/restitution/obliquity sweep;
18 mixed contact/bilateral/nonnegative cases across mass scale and block order;
normal rebound over masses `1e-9` to `1e9`; static midpoint reversal; singular
tangent response; global mode promotion; rotated tangent bases; and sticky fault,
empty-count and recovery sequences. GPU solve tolerance in these fixtures is
`2e-5` physical row velocity, with independent checks at `3e-5`; these are not the
much tighter CPU f64 gates or a sustained-rest/large-island performance certificate.

**Not connected to `RigidWorld` yet.** The existing GPU tangential response uses
two rows per block and penalty-determined friction radii. The next integration
must assemble all three impact rows, track contact episodes on device, suppress
only onset penalty work, handle position/energy correction, publish physical
impulses into reactions/break sampling, and preserve mutation/rollback precision
without host substep round trips. The runtime's nonzero-restitution rejection is

wrapper selects three rows per contact and the midpoint solver rather than a
fixed-radius two-row disk solve. There is no second copy of the articulated mass
solver or a host impact solve inside dispatch.

The common response shader now uses the selected block width for projection,
matrix slots, free velocity, application and readout. Impact input supplies normal
plus two orthonormal tangent directions, static/dynamic coefficients, restitution
and predicted incoming normal speed. Surface motion contributes only tangentially.

acceleration once, then exports full normal-plus-tangent world impulses. Scalar
impulses retain the existing `CoulombDiskSolution` readout layout for integration
with joint reactions. Unconnected articulations preserve their predicted rates.

Impact island selection differs deliberately from penalty-friction selection:
an active impact row participates even when penalty force and friction are both
zero. Fixed ground does not union otherwise disconnected dynamic groups. A supplied
active contact with no mobile endpoint faults explicitly instead of disappearing.

The caller still supplies the approaching impact active set; separating predicted
contacts fail closed rather than silently being reclassified by this component.

preserve and consume the retained increment, as in the existing precision path.

The stage retains an eight-byte record per input contact: inclusion flag plus the
normal-speed bits. Assembly consumes that exact speed for the normal row, rather
than recomputing a potentially different sign at a rounded zero crossing. The
retained-increment route still avoids subtracting rounded large background rates.
There is one additional retained buffer and pipeline; encoding introduces no host
allocation, submission or readback. The shared response layout now requires 32
storage-buffer bindings; constructor validation reflects that requirement.

The graph keeps every active contact edge when forming dynamic groups, including
separating contacts. It then marks roots with an onset and at least one eligible
predicted contact. Only nonseparating contact rows and those roots' scalar rows are
packed. Filtered rows consume no solve capacity and retain zero impulse output.
An onset group with no eligible contacts contributes no velocity or scalar solve;
this does not discard its episode history or replace the still-needed position stage.
Standalone impact constructors retain their strict caller-supplied active-set contract.

## P4/P5 GPU mass-weighted position response — linearized component checkpoint

Added `ResidentImpactPositionResponse` and `ImpactPositionConfig` using the common
articulated mass/Jacobian/island/Gram machinery. This stage solves displacement
corrections at the input pose, not physical impulses:

- Only new episode rows with positive depth become normal position constraints.
  Persistent contacts remain connectivity edges but do not change the spring's
  rest depth or receive another onset position correction.
- Position rows are nonnegative scalar blocks with one normal direction and two
  zero padding rows. They share the solve with bilateral/nonnegative joint position
  rows. Friction, restitution and physical predictor/boundary velocities do not
  enter the displacement equation.
- Position island selection retains scalar corrections for onset groups even when
  the new contact depth is zero. Velocity selection still requires an eligible
  nonseparating contact; the two stages have different inclusion conditions.
- The output is generalized displacement. Its debug solution layout reports
  displacement multipliers and linearized residuals; these must not be published
  as contact impulses or joint reaction forces. Physical input rates remain unchanged.

Added typed `ScalarPositionBuffers`, separate from velocity-constraint buffers.
`DistanceGpu` now exports geometric position residuals alongside its existing
velocity rows, sharing the original Jacobians. Distance minimum/maximum/equality,
zero-distance anchor coincidence, cone rows and scalar axis stops supply their
signed gaps directly. Reconstructing a gap by subtracting a large constraint rate
from the velocity residual is deliberately avoided. This adds one retained export
buffer and no additional export dispatch; the distance layout requires 23 storage
bindings and validates the device limit.

Initial evidence in
`benchmarks/primitives/impact-position-gpu-2026-09-28/`:

  articulated oracle covers onset masks, unilateral/bilateral scalar rows, endpoint
  reversal, offset COM/off-diagonal inertia, a floating hinge chain and a driven
  boundary. Peak displacement error is **`4.869755827969016e-9`** against CPU response.
- Generated joint geometry is compared with independent CPU preparation for seven
  cases: radial equality, radial minimum, radial maximum, zero-distance equality,
  locked spherical cone, prismatic stop and revolute stop.
- A `1.0001` versus `1` radial gap survives an input speed of `1e8`, where the same
  gap is lost from the f32 velocity residual. Two timesteps and zero/nonzero onset
  depths yield the same radial displacement; source contact rows and physical
  rates are unchanged.
- Redundant normal rows release the shallower multiplier and close the deeper
  linearized gap at masses `1e-6`, `1` and `1e6`. Invalid tolerances, onset masks and
  depths fail closed; sticky faults and no-onset updates retire displacement output.
- `first-regressions.log`: the existing seven articulated-impact and six mixed
  joint/contact GPU tests passed after introducing the shared position mode.

`components-final.log` records **40 passing GPU component tests**: four position,

This is **not position application or live GPU restitution**. The next boundary

## P4/P5 GPU coordinate displacement and redrift — component checkpoint

Added `FeatherstoneKernel::apply_position_displacement` and the solver wrapper
`FeatherstoneSolver::apply_position_displacement_gpu`. The existing Featherstone
integration shader now has a position-only mode:

- A retained generalized displacement buffer replaces the predictor-delta binding
  for this dispatch. No extra storage binding, pipeline or uniform buffer is added;
  the predictor's physical velocity increment remains unchanged.
- Input coordinates, physical rates, body poses and translation residues are copied
  to a separate projected state. Displacements use the existing joint-coordinate
  and normalized-quaternion integration formulas at unit scale. Physical joint
  rates are restored before FK reconstructs body velocities at the projected pose.
- The mode skips force integration, velocity caps and legacy unilateral coordinate
  clamps. Coupled position rows must supply the displacement constraints. Authored
  scalar equality coordinates remain locked. This is linearized position
  application, not a general nonlinear bound/manifold projection certificate.
- Prescribed bodies do not advance during projection. Ordinary redrift starts
  from that projected input and advances them once using the actual timestep.
  Articulations with zero displacement preserve their copied state exactly.
- Coordinate/FK translation compensation is copied through the projected state.
  Nonfinite displacement input sets sticky fault bit 31; bit 30 remains reserved
  for runtime break interruption. Full frame rollback remains the caller's job.
- Six cached state-binding sets cover ping-pong prediction, projection and redrift
  without warmed-up bind-group creation. Position application itself creates no
  additional retained buffers or pipelines; the caller supplies its projected state.

The CPU impact hook previously sent position displacement through velocity caps.
`featherstone_integrate.rs` now takes an explicit rate-capping switch, disabled only
for the impact position application. Ordinary dynamics and physical redrift retain
their prior caps. A CPU regression checks scalar, ball, free, distance and D6 joints
with displacement `0.25` and velocity limit `1e-6`, including quaternion updates.
Other existing CPU angular/coordinate projection rules are unchanged; general
nonlinear CPU/GPU position parity still needs certification.

It consumes typed velocity-impact and persistent-friction responses with matching
model/contact/scalar ordering. Position-response objects are not accepted:

- Contact world impulses and scalar solution records are selected in original row
  order, including active zero-impulse constraints. Overlapping active slots fail.
- Generalized physical response increments are combined without adding predictor
  changes. Overlapping nonzero DOF increments fail rather than being double-counted.

  and inactive-output retirement before a separate merge pass writes outputs.
  Every encode clears the outputs first; existing or newly detected faults leave

## Automatic detachment preserves existing contact episodes

The live breakage regression exposed a CPU episode-lifecycle error, not evidence
that the new GPU merge path is integrated. `body_structure_stamp` changes when a
support joint breaks. The existing CPU contact cache interpreted that structural
change as a fresh approaching contact on the next substep, suppressed its penalty
load, and applied a second position projection. This also occurred with zero
restitution. The old GPU penalty path did not perform that extra projection.

`ImpactCache::preserve_after_detachment` now refreshes structural stamps after an
automatic break while retaining existing pair history. Collider stamps, local
poses and explicit body-state edit stamps must still match. New pairs are not
inserted by this operation, and explicit state/material edits still retire their
episodes. The frame checkpoint retains the pre-break cache for failure rollback.

## Live GPU impact integration — acceptance in progress

`RuntimeContacts` now owns stable episode identities/history, velocity impact and
excluded-group friction stages, the physical merge, a position-response stage and
a separate projected state. Normal row generation, episode suppression and normal
force gathering precede prediction. Impact, friction, merge and position solves
follow prediction and scalar-row export. Merged physical outputs feed joint scalar
publication and reactions; only position output reaches the projected-state pass.
The corrected physical rates are redrifted from that projected state.

The projected state is registered with coordinate/FK compensation before any
bindings capture those buffers. Its contents are overwritten from input state on
every position application. Episode history is checkpointed before a segment,
inherited across recompilation, and restored from the original compiled frame on
post-break failure. A checkpoint-valid flag prevents an early failure from
restoring a stale previous-frame checkpoint. Automatic detachment refreshes only
matching structural identities; explicit state edits update device identity tokens
without requiring a model rebuild.

Contact readout now separates normal and tangential components of the merged
impulse and classifies impact friction from final physical slip, not the midpoint
law's sticking flag. Failure-only diagnostic readback identifies the response stage,
island, iteration count and raw residual. The GPU contract test continues to check
fail-closed unsupported mutations using body damping instead of restitution.

## Zero-depth sphere-box episodes and sequential breaks

The sequential-break diagnostic (`sequential-diagnostics.log`) isolated the second
support event at substep 1: GPU reaction 70.0000076 N versus CPU 31.1 N. CPU
sphere-box collision retained an exact-touch zero-depth row at substep 0; GPU
sphere-box collision discarded it. At the next penetrating substep only the GPU
classified a fresh impact, rather than retaining the existing penalty episode.

An initial attempt to discard exact touching on CPU made the sequential fixture
pass (`sequential-fixed.log`), but the CPU aggregate rejected it: the existing
weight-support fixture remained at height 0.5 rather than its analytic compressed
equilibrium. That attempt is **reverted**, not an accepted fix. Its first geometry
reproduction, intermediate results and failed aggregate remain in `touch-first.log`,
`touch-fixed.log` and `cpu-aggregate-touch.log`. The superseded GPU breakage rerun
in `breakage-touch-fixed.log` was deliberately terminated after changing approach;
it is not acceptance evidence.

The retained implementation preserves zero-depth sphere-box manifolds on GPU.
Normal rows accept nonnegative depth and keep response eligibility for episode
classification, while zero-depth rows produce neither spring nor compression
damping force. CPU sphere-box geometry and its existing settling acceptance are
unchanged. Exact touching and small positive/negative gaps are now explicit geometry
cases, and a CPU two-step oracle verifies penalty support rather than a repeated
onset impulse. The sequential-break test now additionally checks the independent
32 N / 31.1 N reaction oracles, without changing its 0.002 N CPU/GPU tolerance.

Evidence in `benchmarks/primitives/impact-history-gpu-2026-09-29/`:

- `touch-retained-cpu.log`: ten existing contact/settling tests and thirteen runtime
  restitution tests pass, including the new zero-depth lifecycle oracle.
- `touch-retained-geometry-gpu.log`: the sphere-box analytic GPU fixture passes,
  including zero-depth rows at three scales and both endpoint orders.
- `touch-retained-normal-gpu.log`: all four normal-contact GPU tests pass, including
  drop/settling, faults, material/wrench parity and resident pipeline chaining.
- `sequential-retained-gpu.log`: the original sequential-break fixture passes
  (40.31 s), including both analytic reaction oracles and the unchanged parity gate.
- `cpu-aggregate-retained.log`: **414 passing test executions across 43 suites**,
  no failures and seven correctly ignored GPU cases. `check-retained.log` and
  `git diff --check` pass; only existing test-helper dead-code warnings remain.
- `retained-runtime-regressions.log`: all five full breakage tests pass (290.28 s).
  Its chained restitution invocation stopped on a transient manifest error while
  the benchmark target was being added; no restitution tests ran in that invocation.
- `retained-restitution-mixed.log`: all five live restitution tests pass, including
  the new one-second CPU/GPU resting-support fixture checking trajectory, 20 N support
  and analytic 0.4998 m equilibrium height (312.83 s). All eight mixed-contact tests
  also pass (470.15 s), serialized after restitution.

Other shape families' exact-touch conventions are not generalized by this fix.

## Live runtime benchmark harness (P6, partial)

### Allocation/transfer instrumentation source audit

The current cached dependency is wgpu 29.0.3. Its Vulkan backend declares and
default-initializes `memory_allocations_counter`, but the only subsequent
reference in that backend copies its value into `get_internal_counters()`;
there is no increment/decrement wiring. Consequently, the existing zero raw
HAL allocation count cannot establish a zero allocation total or a peak.
This is an upstream counter limitation, not evidence that the runtime allocated
nothing. No dependency source or pin was changed.

The same public `Device::generate_allocator_report()` API exposes allocation
entries, blocks, allocated bytes and reserved bytes when its backend supports
reports; unsupported configurations return `None`. The cached Vulkan
implementation delegates to its allocator's report. This is a concrete route
for a future hardware-backed allocation oracle, but it has not been executed
against the current adapter yet and a frame-boundary snapshot still does not
prove a transient high-water mark. Sampling and coverage must include resource
creation/rebuilds and staging, not just end-of-frame publication.

Transfer coverage must include `molla-storage::Buffer::upload_with_scratch`,
model/control compilation and parameter/identity writes in the retained kernels,
not just `GpuRuntimeDiagnostics`' state totals. The five storage/sim/kernel/
geometry/solver source trees contain 915 matching write/init/map/view source lines;
that inventory is not a claim that all are reachable from this benchmark.
The existing measured scope remains explicit: runtime state diagnostics only,
with complete totals and transient peaks unavailable. The matrix must not be
presented as complete before that scope is repaired and validated.

`make bench-primitives` now runs the `runtime_primitives` benchmark through
`nixVulkan`, defaulting to release mode, 20 warm-up frames and 1,000 measured frames
at dt=1/240 s / four substeps. The matrix defaults to 1, 100, 1,000 and 10,000
instances of distance, loaded cone, D6 drive, reaction, breaking, friction and mixed
scenes. Cases use the public live `RigidWorld` runtime, not ModelBuilder-only solver
timings. The mixed fixture includes friction coupled to a D6 drive plus distance,
cone and reaction bodies, and exactly one break armed halfway through measurement.
The break-only fixture checks one event per instance.

Each case/backend/count uses a fresh child process; the parent serializes workers,
reports failed exit statuses/signals and continues the matrix. Capacity/numerical
errors remain failures, and a process signal is not automatically labelled OOM.
GPU cases reject software adapters and require timestamp features; no fallback is
allowed. `Engine::new_gpu_with_features` supplies explicit opt-in features while
the existing constructors retain their empty feature request. `AdapterInfo` now
also exposes backend-provided `driver_info` for version details.

Output includes setup/frame-loop wall time, maximum frame time, GPU device timeline
span, device/driver metadata, settings, articulation/body counts, break counts,
model compilation counts, state transfer counters and post-frame observed allocation
maxima. The measurement scopes are explicit: timestamps include host/queue idle,
state counters exclude other uploads, and boundary-observed allocations are not true
transient peaks. At this first checkpoint dispatch counts, total transfers and
transient peak allocations were **unavailable**; dispatch instrumentation is now
implemented below. Total transfers and transient peaks remain open. This harness
is not full P6 completion.

## Encoded GPU dispatch metrics and first GPU benchmark execution

`molla-core/gpu-metrics` adds a thread-local `DispatchScope`, enabled by the solver's
existing `resource-counters` feature. Recording calls compile to no-ops without
that feature. Scopes reject nesting, reset on drop/unwind, isolate threads and
report overflow. Counts describe Molla-encoded dispatch commands, not completed
shader invocations, workgroup counts or opaque backend-generated commands.

There are 37 instrumented encoding sites in 24 source files: runtime contact/
impact/island/publication/reaction/constraint stages, Featherstone/CRBA/Jacobian/
reaction kernels, precision transfers, narrow/bounds/LBVH stages and radix sorting.
`dispatch-sites.txt` records the source audit: every listed direct dispatch has one
adjacent recording call and no indirect dispatch sites occur in those files.
The benchmark scopes only measured frames, including break-triggered recompilation.

Evidence in `benchmarks/primitives/impact-history-gpu-2026-09-29/`:

- `dispatch-counter-unit.log`: five scope lifecycle/nesting/thread/overflow tests pass.
- `dispatch-runtime-gpu.log`: the live-runtime GPU counter oracle passes (69.28 s).
  One or 32 fixed bodies use one predictor dispatch per substep without readout,
  and five with reaction readout, at one and four substeps. No measured frame
  recompiles its model. The new CPU/GPU metric gates are included in the aggregates.
- `dispatch-cpu-smoke.log`: all seven CPU smoke cases pass under schema 2 with
  zero encoded GPU dispatches.
- `cpu-aggregate-dispatch.log`: **419 passing test executions across 44 suites**,
  no failures and seven correctly ignored GPU cases.
- `dispatch-check-final.log`: the explicit resource-counter all-target check passes.
- `dispatch-check-workspace.log`, `dispatch-format-check.log` and `git diff --check`
  pass; the workspace check retains only existing test-helper dead-code warnings.
- `bench-gpu-smoke.log`: the serialized release matrix ran on RTX 4080 / Vulkan /
  NVIDIA 595.91.07 with two warm-up and four measured frames, one instance each.
  Distance, cone, reaction, break and friction completed with positive GPU timestamp
  spans and respectively 144, 144, 80, 97 and 1,680 encoded dispatches. The break
  case published exactly one event. These are smoke checks, not the required
  1,000-frame performance matrix or uncontended timing acceptance.

The GPU smoke aggregate **failed**, correctly: D6 and mixed fixtures both stop at
warm-up step zero with `GPU stable feedback requires scalar drive coordinates`.
The public world enables stable feedback by default; the kernel currently rejects
multi-DOF feedback modes, even a D6 linear velocity drive. Neither fixture has been
weakened to a slider, disabled feedback or substituted CPU execution. This is an
implementation gap to fix before the full matrix. Relevant code is
`crates/molla-kernels/src/featherstone.rs` and
`crates/molla-kernels/shaders/featherstone_feedback.wgsl`. The ordinary GPU drive
assembly also uses zero position for non-scalar joints; CPU `motor_coordinate`
instead reads translations or XYZ Euler angles from the stored quaternion. Merely
removing the host rejection is therefore not sufficient for general D6 feedback.

The same run exposed an unavailable backend allocation statistic: raw HAL
`memory_allocations` stayed zero while buffer memory was nonzero. Schema 3 now
reports `None` rather than claiming zero allocations, adds observed live-buffer
counts and bounds timestamp readback polling to 120 seconds. Its focused reaction
rerun in `bench-gpu-schema3.log` passes: 80 encoded dispatches, a positive timestamp
span, 86 observed live buffers and `None` for backend allocation count. The prior
schema-2 allocation zeros are not valid physical allocation counts. Do not rebuild
the benchmark executable while its parent is running; child workers reuse it.

### Multi-DOF feedback coordinate repair and retained benchmarks

The preceding D6/mixed rejection is now repaired, rather than bypassed. Ordinary
and stabilized GPU motor assembly share the CPU coordinate convention: scalar
coordinates, Free/D6 translations and XYZ Euler angles for quaternion rotations.
The stabilization kernel retains its coupled mass-response solve and force caps;
the host still rejects stable feedback without rigorous dynamics. Position
coordinates are evaluated only for position-containing modes or cable springs.

- `multidof-first-runtime.log` preserves the original nonzero-target equilibrium

  rejection would have left the ordinary position-drive error intact.
- `multidof-final-gpu.log`: the new live-runtime D6/Free/Ball oracle passes all
  24 phases, with stabilization off/on, nonzero equilibrium targets and one-second
  simultaneous position, velocity and combined-drive trajectories. Fixtures use

  CPU/GPU frame pairs retain 1e-3 pose/rate gates, a 0.02 summed reaction-difference
  gate and unchanged model-compilation counts across control edits (112.54 s).
- `feedback-regressions-gpu.log`: all three retained feedback regressions pass
  (204.22 s), including rigorous-dynamics rejection, nonfinite-gain fault handling,
  effort caps, momentum and the 512-step stiff trajectory.
- `cpu-aggregate-multidof.log`: 419 passing executions across 44 suites, seven
  ignored GPU tests; this predates the new angular-limit oracle below.
- `multidof-check.log`: workspace check passes with existing helper warnings.
- `bench-d6-fixed.log` and `bench-mixed-fixed.log`: both CPU and GPU release workers

`test-primitives-multidof-feedback-gpu` is included in the GPU aggregate. Its
adjacent angular-limit oracle independently composes XYZ rotations and checks
that clipping one D6 angle preserves the others and authored endpoint frames.
The CPU oracle passes (`multidof-limits-cpu.log`). The GPU oracle failed on its
first axis (`multidof-limits-first-gpu.log`): the shader decomposed Rx*Ry*Rz but
recomposed Rz*Ry*Rx. Correcting the product order passes all three unchanged
1e-5-radian GPU gates (`multidof-limits-fixed-gpu.log`, 102.93 s). The new CPU
near-gimbal oracle also passes for both pitch signs and each independently
clipped axis (`multidof-limits-expanded-cpu.log`). Its GPU reproduction fails by
0.1999997 radians (`multidof-near-gimbal-first-gpu.log`): the old `abs(sin(y))`
threshold collapses resolvable angles 0.003 radians from gimbal lock. Extraction
now uses `atan2(m02, length(m00, m01))` with a 16-f32-epsilon cosine threshold,
matching the CPU algorithm's structure rather than prematurely discarding roll.
The combined GPU feedback/limit rerun passes (`multidof-complete-gpu.log`): all
24 feedback phases (112.29 s), the three original projection cases, and all six
near-gimbal cases (303.43 s for both limit tests). Maximum near-gimbal orientation
error is 5.76e-6 radians, below the unchanged 1e-3 gate.

The CPU aggregate including both new limit oracles passes **421 executions across
45 suites**, with seven ignored GPU cases (`cpu-aggregate-limits.log`). Workspace
checking and scoped formatting pass (`multidof-limits-check.log`,
`multidof-limits-format.log`). A further analytic D6 fixture covers all six axes,
free/bounded/locked, in both effort directions with rotated endpoint frames:
36 independent articulations over one second, 240 frames, two substeps. Its CPU
gate passes with peak summed pose error 9.43e-8 and rate error 5.50e-13
(`d6-axis-cpu.log`). The matching GPU test passes in 34.45 s with peak summed pose
error 6.82e-5 and rate error 1.34e-4, below its unchanged 1e-3 gates
(`d6-axis-gpu.log`). The fixture is included in both aggregate lanes via
`runtime_d6_axis_certification`.
The subsequent CPU aggregate passes **422 executions across 46 suites**, with
seven ignored GPU cases (`cpu-aggregate-d6-axis.log`), and the workspace check
including this new fixture passes (`d6-axis-check.log`).

The default release benchmark matrix was launched through
`NVIDIA_VERSION=595.91.07 nix develop --impure -c make bench-primitives`, with no
other Molla tests/benchmarks running and 0% reported GPU utilization immediately
before launch. It requests all seven fixtures, both backends and 1/100/1,000/10,000
instances, 20 warm-up and 1,000 measured frames. `bench-full-matrix.log` is its
partial evidence, not a completed matrix. Existing desktop/remote-desktop
processes were left untouched. Total transfers and transient allocation peaks
remain explicitly unavailable, so even successful case timings do not finish P6.

The run reached five successful cases: distance CPU/GPU at 1 and 100 instances,
then CPU at 1,000 instances (26.9702 s measured). The 1,000-instance GPU worker
then stalled. The kernel log explicitly reports **NVIDIA Xid 109, CTX SWITCH
TIMEOUT**, naming that worker PID 896062 (`bench-distance-1000-xid.log`). Its
process remained alive in a poll wait, with unchanged CPU time and idle GPU;
absence of new benchmark output was not treated as termination. A debugger attach
was denied (`bench-distance-1000-wait-stack.log`); no ptrace policy was changed.
Only the owned benchmark process group was terminated after preserving the driver
fault evidence; its session exited 143. No desktop process, driver configuration
or GPU reset was touched. The 1,000-instance GPU case has **no passing result**,
and all subsequent matrix cases are unrun. The driver timeout's root cause remains
unproven; do not diagnose it as OOM or simply retry the full matrix unchanged.

### Public runtime examples

`crates/molla-solvers/examples/runtime_primitives.rs` now contains independent
public-API examples for distance, a loaded cone, fixed support reaction, one-shot
breakage, explicit static/dynamic contact materials and a combined-target D6
drive. It does not import benchmark fixtures or rely on USD assets. The paired
`examples/README.md` records authoring/readout calls, units, endpoint conventions,
readout invalidation, event draining and the rolling-versus-sliding distinction.
New `example-primitives` / `example-primitives-gpu` Make targets select CPU or GPU
explicitly, with no CPU substitution if GPU selection cannot be satisfied.

After the faulted matrix was terminated, all six CPU examples passed
(`examples-cpu.log`), including 20 N distance/fixed support readouts, a loaded
cone at its 0.25-radian boundary, one drained break event with no repeat, contact
material/rolling readout and a responding combined-target D6 drive. The workspace
all-target check also passed (`examples-check.log`), with existing helper warnings.
Formatting and `git diff --check` pass. A fresh one-body GPU reaction example
passes after the driver-faulted worker is gone (`examples-reaction-gpu.log`),
without a GPU reset. All six GPU examples then pass (`examples-all-gpu.log`),
including 20 N support, a single break event, rolling contact and D6 response.
This proves small fresh contexts still execute, not that the scale failure is fixed.
No concurrent build/test was launched during the matrix, and its worker executable
was not rebuilt while running. These remain provisional API usage artifacts, not
a completed P6 handoff or numerical acceptance substitutes.

### Benchmark worker supervision

The benchmark parent no longer waits indefinitely for each worker. A configurable
`--case-timeout-seconds` budget (default 3,600 seconds, strictly positive) includes
worker setup, warm-up and measurement. Timeout terminates/reaps only that worker,
records `case_process_timeout` and stops with an error; remaining cases are unrun.
Ordinary completed-process failures still preserve their exit status and allow
the remaining cases. This is process supervision, not a repair or suppression of
the underlying GPU timeout, and no timeout result is reported as OOM or a pass.

Two subprocess tests verify successful/failed statuses and timeout termination/
reaping (`bench-process-tests-final.log`; one separately ignored child fixture).
They are included in the CPU aggregate. A feature-enabled all-target check passes
(`bench-process-check.log`). Setup/warm-up completion records and optional
`--trace-frames` now expose the last started phase/frame; the CPU trace smoke
passes (`bench-process-trace-cpu.log`). Traced runs include logging overhead and
are explicitly diagnostic, not performance measurements.
An end-to-end CPU-only timeout test also passes as an expected failure
(`bench-process-timeout-cpu.log`): a one-second budget terminates/reaps the first
1,000-instance debug worker, returns nonzero, and never starts the requested
subsequent one-instance case. This fixture tests supervision, not CPU capacity or
performance. The first full-workspace attempt is preserved in
`workspace-test-all.log`. Compilation completes (8m 07s), then the all-target
suite reaches `bench_sensor_physics_latency` and fails adapter discovery with
`active_backends: Backends(0x0)`. Unlike `test-gpu` and `harden`'s final gate,
`test-all` did not apply the existing `RUN_WITH` wrapper, even though default
workspace features include GPU and all-target execution runs GPU benchmarks.
The recipe now uses `$(RUN_WITH)` without dropping targets or changing features.
The rerun in `workspace-test-all-wrapped.log` now discovers RTX 4080 / Vulkan,
completes all 24 sensor-physics latency cases and advances into subsequent
workspace suites. It then fails the contact-quadruped test described below, after
1,318 passes across 261 completed passing suites (696 ignored cases), followed by
three passing tests and one failure in the articulation suite. Neither aggregate
is a passing full-workspace gate.

### Contact-quadruped fixture audit and retained stiction regression

`procedural_quadruped_tree_survives_floor_contacts_while_controlled` failed with
hip coordinate 3.49e-16 against a 0.18-radian target. The unchanged focused
reproduction is `quadruped-contact-first.log`; diagnostics are retained in
`quadruped-contact-loads.log` and `quadruped-contact-state.log`.

The original assertion counted **any** contact as floor coverage. In fact its
eight initial contacts were between connected robot links, with no world endpoint:
four lower/upper-link overlaps and four root/upper-link overlaps. The latter
produce approximately 6,500 N normal force, and enough static-friction torque to
hold the hip drives by more than a tenfold margin. The feet are above the floor,
and the original lower-link rest positions also disagree with zero-coordinate FK
by 0.02 m. Changing `model.default_friction` after building had not changed the
already-authored per-shape 0.5 coefficients. Stationary hips are therefore not
evidence that the drive was ignored or that a floor-convergence gate was exercised.

Both physical situations are now retained in
`tests/featherstone_articulation_cpu.rs`:

- The original unfiltered geometry, targets, gains, timestep and 800-frame duration
  remain as a separate stiction regression. It verifies there is no floor contact,
  checks the 6,500 N preload and Coulomb torque budget, requires the four hips to
  remain stationary within 1e-9 rad, and requires the knees to keep responding.
  Its maximum hip motion is 3.53e-16 rad. No original self-contact is disabled in
  this retained fixture.
- The floor fixture uses FK-consistent rest poses, explicitly excludes only
  overlapping directly connected shape pairs, and starts each foot with 1e-4 m
  floor penetration. Builder-authored friction is explicitly 0.7 on both sides.
  Actual acted world-endpoint contacts and a 10 N peak preload within 1% are
  required, rather than treating self-contact counts as floor proof. Motor gains,
  targets, duration and the original convergence/finite-state thresholds remain
  unchanged. It exercises three floor-contact frames and reaches hip 0.17025 rad
  for the 0.18-radian target, with 10 N peak floor force.

All five articulation tests pass (`quadruped-contact-fixed.log`). This repairs an
invalid test fixture/expectation under static friction; no engine friction law was
weakened to make a blocked hip move. The suite is now part of the primitive CPU
aggregate. The fresh aggregate passes 429 tests across 48 suites, with eight
ignored tests (`cpu-aggregate-quadruped.log`), and `make check-all` passes
(`quadruped-check.log`). The full workspace gate still needs a successful rerun.
