### Control-body-wrench consumption and owner lookup

The source audit confirmed that CPU Featherstone consumed state-body forces but
omitted `Control::body_external_f`, while the GPU live runtime rejected nonzero
control-body wrenches. Merely subtracting that control field in inverse dynamics
would fabricate reaction loads without applying the force to forward dynamics.

The current implementation adds world-space COM control wrenches exactly once
in the CPU/GPU predictors and in the corresponding reaction external-load
assembly. The original state-force and control buffers stay separate and are
not accumulated back into persistent state. GPU input is another retained
storage binding, not a per-body CPU solve or per-substep readback; existing
control uploads refresh it without structural recompilation. The former runtime
rejection is removed; selected acceptance fixtures now pass. Empty control force
arrays remain optional in the lower-level solver; nonempty mismatched counts
and nonfinite/overflowing total loads produce errors.

New fixtures in `runtime_body_control_wrenches.rs` cover state-plus-control load
superposition, offset-COM fixed reactions, edits/removal without accumulation,
break-trigger loads and continued free motion, one-second free acceleration and
rotation, and ten-second contact holding followed by analytic sliding. The first
CPU run passes three new control tests and all 12 runtime-reaction tests,
including independent articulation loads before/after deletion and compaction
(`body-control-first-cpu.log`). Both accumulation-helper tests pass
(`body-control-helper-cpu.log`). All four initial GPU tests pass in 101.19 s
(`body-control-first-gpu.log`), including optional empty-control binding for a
zero-DOF fixed joint. The fallback storage now has a 32-byte minimum suitable for
a spatial wrench. An unused import reported in this first GPU run was moved into
the private test module that uses it. The completed 10,000-instance benchmark
used the frozen executable from before
these control-wrench changes, identified by `featherstone-scale-environment.log`.
The benchmark process has completed and been reaped. The CPU primitive aggregate
passes 433 tests across 49 suites, with eight ignored tests
(`body-control-aggregate-cpu.log`), and `make check-all` passes
(`body-control-check.log`). Additional overflow/failure/recovery tests pass on
CPU along with all 13 body-enable/quarantine tests (`body-control-complete-cpu.log`).
The extended GPU run passes all five tests in 104.66 seconds
(`body-control-complete-gpu.log`), including overflow rollback/recovery, ten-second
holding and sliding, fixed support/break continuation, free motion, and optional
empty-control bindings. A final all-target workspace check and scoped formatting
check pass (`body-control-final-check.log`, `body-control-final-format.log`).

The isolated CPU scale case completed setup in 523.748 seconds and measurement
in 1,189.606 seconds. A source audit found that each CPU reaction substep scans every
authored joint separately for every articulation, producing an O(A×J) owner
lookup even for independent one-joint systems. The current source groups authored
joints once by articulation CSR range, retaining per-articulation authored order
and existing RNEA evaluation. A heterogeneous 16-articulation reaction/compaction
regression passes in the CPU suite above. This is a source-grounded quadratic-path
repair; the completed 10,000-instance benchmark uses the old owner-lookup
implementation and remains the unmodified baseline.
The unchanged 1,000-instance CPU/GPU distance benchmark passes against the new
source (`bench-distance-1000-grouped-reactions.log`, metadata in
`body-control-environment.log`). CPU measured wall time drops from 25.5041 s to
15.8704 s; GPU measured wall time is 3.38535 s (previously 3.35833 s), with the
same 36,000 dispatches, two compilations and state-transfer counts. These are
single-run before/after measurements of the owner-grouping plus control-wrench
changes, not a universal speedup claim or a new 10,000-instance result.

The full workspace `make test-all` gate is being rerun against this source
(`workspace-test-all-body-controls.log`). Earlier full-workspace failures are
not superseded until this aggregate finishes successfully. The explicit
feature-enabled benchmark `cargo test` help invocation also succeeds

### Authored-root momentum certification — failing CPU gate

`runtime_com_roots.rs` now tests unconstrained authored Free and D6 roots with
nonidentity parent/child rotations, a child-anchor offset distinct from the COM,
and a full off-diagonal inertia. The body has mass 2 kg, COM `(0.2,-0.1,0.3)`,
initial COM velocity `(0.1,0.2,-0.3)` and angular velocity `(0.3,-0.2,0.1)`.
Both endpoint frames must remain exactly as authored. No gravity, contact,
external wrench, drive or damping is applied. The oracle checks world linear
momentum and angular momentum about the COM over one second, with four substeps
and frame timesteps 1/60, 1/120 and 1/240 s. Each relative-error denominator is
the initial momentum magnitude, with an absolute scale floor of `1e-3`; the plan's
CPU/GPU relative limits remain `1e-6`/`1e-3`.

`authored-root-baseline-cpu.log` demonstrates a failure for both joint kinds:

| Frames | Peak relative linear error | Peak relative angular error |
|---|---|---|
| 60 | 1.0237483066003215e-4 | 6.586207737533928e-5 |
| 120 | 5.1185027348781706e-5 | 3.293276154368058e-5 |
| 240 | 2.5591916184174987e-5 | 1.646681088475744e-5 |

The approximately first-order timestep convergence does not satisfy the declared
gate. The existing implicit-root COM-edit test still passes. A second run with
reaction readout enabled (`authored-root-reactions-cpu.log`) reproduces the same
momentum errors while the unconstrained root's transmitted force and torque stay
below `1e-6`. That zero-reaction invariant is retained in the acceptance test;
fixing coordinate integration must not fabricate a support load. This new test is
retained as a failing acceptance test, not ignored or weakened. GPU execution
passes its declared `1e-3` gate (`authored-root-first-gpu.log`): both GPU tests
pass, including all six new kind/timestep cases, on the wrapped GPU path. The
worst new relative errors are 1.0256808502914725e-4 linear and
6.619318282829433e-5 angular. GPU and CPU show comparable first-order drift;
the looser GPU threshold passes while the CPU threshold still fails. The
GPU-feature compilation check also passes (`authored-root-feature-check.log`).
`authored-root-first-cpu.log` contains
an earlier test-only compilation error (`Transform` composition uses `compose`,
not multiplication), corrected before the measured run. No solver change has yet
been made for this newly quantified integration defect.

The repair must also preserve stage conventions: `joint_reactions::sample_cpu`
currently derives generalized acceleration from the input/output rate difference
and evaluates RNEA at the input pose. `FeatherstoneSolver::drift_cpu_mode` can
redrift an already predicted rate after constraint correction. Simply replacing
the published rate with a momentum-transported rate inside the shared integrator
would therefore change reaction inputs and subsequent correction stages. The GPU
path likewise separates prediction, correction, drift and reaction dispatch.
These consumers need coordinated treatment rather than a post-step velocity
normalization that only makes the isolated conservation assertion pass.

### CPU floating-articulation momentum transport — validation in progress

The live CPU publication path now integrates the unrestricted floating
articulation's world linear/angular momentum, rather than interpreting the
unchanged old-configuration generalized rates at a rotated/translated new
configuration. `rigid_momentum.rs` derives the instantaneous momentum derivative
from RNEA at the input pose and the corrected generalized-rate increment, with
gravity restored explicitly. It does not assume zero external load or simply
renormalize velocity to an initial magnitude. The discrete target is
`h_next = h_input + dt * h_dot_input`.

The articulation centroid advances by `dt * P_next / mass`; a uniform root
translation retains every internal joint coordinate. A composite-inertia solve
then maps the target spatial momentum into the output root's six rates, retaining
all descendant relative rates. The solve checks its attainable inertia range.
Only enabled Free/D6 roots without finite root bounds/caps and with all dynamic
bodies use this transport; immovable/anchored/restricted systems retain their
existing integration. Selected sleeping articulations are respected, and
unmodified body-velocity records are restored exactly after reconstruction.

This runs after substep constraint correction and reaction sampling in both live
CPU paths, before publication. Reaction/break thresholds therefore keep their
force-evaluation rate convention. Published distance/cone geometry is refreshed
after transport. The low-level Featherstone predictor and the GPU path have not
been changed by this stage; GPU porting and full mixed/impact acceptance remain
open, not satisfied by this CPU implementation.

An initial rates-only version restored linear momentum but left COM drift and
angular-momentum-about-COM errors up to 7.5497818839899746e-6
(`root-momentum-transport-first-cpu.log`, failing). Advancing the centroid as well
resolves the original six Free/D6 cases without weakening either invariant:

1.2848533253359646e-14. Zero root reaction still passes. All 18 tests in the
root, control-body-wrench and joint-reaction suites pass
(`root-momentum-centroid-cpu.log`). The full CPU aggregate is running
(`root-momentum-aggregate-cpu.log`); wider loads, articulated chains, impacts and
resource effects still need validation before treating the repair as complete.

The full GPU regression run began before these CPU changes; later tests may

`rigid_momentum_gpu.rs` and `shaders/rigid_momentum.wgsl` now provide retained
device-only transport. One invocation handles one articulation with scratch sized
to the model's largest articulation (maximum 32), not total scene size. Immutable
packed records retain frames, COMs, inertia, parent indices and active columns;
the existing device articulation mask handles sleeping selection. Two cached
ping-pong groups and one substep dispatch are added when an eligible floating
articulation exists, without any new substep readback or CPU physics fallback.

The shader derives the inertial momentum increment from the physical corrected
rate-delta buffer and input spatial recurrence, preserving small increments that
would disappear in subtraction of rounded rates. It retains the projected
configuration's geometric momentum-map change, advances the centroid, solves the
composite COM inertia, and applies a uniform world twist through the root rates
and body velocities. Descendant relative rates and internal coordinates remain
unchanged. Compensated body positions and root translation residues are updated
with forced-round two-sum arithmetic, and relative COMs include position residues.
Invalid/nonfinite or out-of-range momentum sets the existing numeric-fault bit 1;
the runtime's frame rollback remains authoritative.

The pass is encoded **after reaction sampling and before the break-halt pass**.
It transports the first breaking substep, then skips every later halted substep;
allowing the break-stop status unconditionally would incorrectly transport those
later substeps again. The no-readout path dispatches the same retained transport
without constructing the reaction pipeline. Exact warm bind-group assertions now
include its two retained groups (13 bare-runtime / 29 distance-runtime groups);
their repeated-frame retention checks are unchanged.

### Singular-inertia hardening regression — CPU repair

The second hardening attempt subsequently fails during its no-default-features
test stage: **1,498 passes, two failures and 895 ignored tests across 337
completed summaries**. Both failures are in `rigid_singular_forces`: a zero
inertia body develops angular velocity near `9.6e17`, and the loaded rotating
rank-two body faults with `floating momentum lies outside inertia range`.
The original fixtures and numerical tolerances remain unchanged.

Two distinct numerical faults are repaired:

- Centroid accumulation previously multiplied and divided an absolute COM even
  for one body. Roundoff left a tiny nonzero COM offset, creating fictitious
  parallel-axis inertia for a point mass. Accumulating offsets from the first
  body COM keeps coincident centers exactly coincident, at any mass scale.
- Positive Cholesky pivots above a cutoff are not proof that all eigenmodes are
  resolved. A rotated rank-two matrix with a nearly singular leading block can
  amplify factorization roundoff and incorrectly pass every pivot test. A new
  independent rotated-nullspace oracle reproduces this at tilt `1e-5` and scale
  `1e-100` (`momentum-singular-factor-baseline.log`). `MassFactor` now accepts
  fresh or imported Cholesky factors only when absolute triangular-solve bounds
  certify the normalized spectrum above the existing relative null cutoff.
  The bound uses `lambda_min >= 1 / (||L^-1||_1 ||L^-1||_infinity)` and the
  normalized matrix's `lambda_max <= n`; inconclusive factors use the existing
  spectral pseudoinverse. No eigenvalue cutoff is loosened or new regularization
  inserted. This adds O(n^2) validation and two n-element temporary vectors at
  factor construction/import; performance must be remeasured.

The exploratory rank-dependent residual bypass did not repair the failure and
was reverted. The transport's original finite/range residual gate is retained,
with richer failure diagnostics. The corrected factor tests pass **16 tests**
(two existing benchmarks ignored), and all **three original singular-force
tests pass** in `momentum-singular-factor-fixed.log` and
`momentum-singular-inertia-fixed-cpu.log`. The centered-only failure remains in
`momentum-singular-centered-cpu.log`. Broader CPU, GPU parity and full hardening
must be rerun after these source changes; the preceding 272-pass GPU run is a
checkpoint before this repair, not certification of later changes.

The complete solver-library CPU lane also passes **123 tests, three ignored**
(`momentum-singular-all-unit-cpu.log`), including retained-factor and impulse
batching coverage. The rotated-nullspace regression additionally checks that
imported Cholesky factors cannot bypass the new conditioning certificate.

The new actual-GPU singular-root test exposed a separate existing limitation:
the six-axis block Cholesky path divides through zero angular pivots. It fails

same centroid anchoring fix in WGSL. The first two failed attempts remain in

Isolated six-axis dynamic roots now use their analytic COM response and the

The intermediate device-Jacobi inverse was replaced rather than adopting a new

### GPU radial-gap precision — independent force oracle

The post-singular-inertia GPU aggregate stopped in

`runtime_distance.wgsl` previously formed the radial gap by subtracting a rounded
length from a rounded bound. The resulting small positional error is amplified
by the velocity correction and force conversion. `distance_gpu.rs` now retains
the authored bound's low part in the radial row's unused `b.w`. The shader forms
the squared-distance difference using exponent scaling, compensated subtractions
and FMA product residues, then divides by the sum of bound and distance. Rounded
intermediates use the existing row-force padding word through atomic store/load;
the force publication restores that word to zero. There are no new allocations,
bindings, dispatches or readbacks. Contact row export shares the same gap path.

The independent new runtime oracle checks the analytic two-body reaction
`direction * gap / (dt^2 * (1/m_a + 1/m_b))`, with masses two and one, initially
stationary bodies, no gravity and no moment arms. It covers 24 scenes: three
dyadic length scales, three coordinate directions plus a diagonal, and positive
and negative sub-ULP bound gaps. The timestep scales with separation so the
requested velocity correction remains above the existing solver's absolute
iteration threshold. Its relative force tolerance is `1e-4` for both backends.

### P5 force/acceleration motor oracle — CPU baseline

`tests/runtime_motor_models.rs` adds a shared CPU/GPU analytic certification

effort modes; and uncapped versus `0.25` physical-force caps. The fixture runs
world-anchored and floating-parent variants with explicit and implicit feedback,
for 384 configurations in total. Each executes ten frames with four substeps.

The oracle independently advances the scalar drive equation, including implicit
stiffness/damping, effective inertia, effort-mode non-scaling and physical caps.
It checks generalized position/rate, the authored physical axis and, for floating
pairs, conserved total linear/angular momentum. Floating parent mass/inertia is
one quarter of the child's, so the effective scalar inertia is one fifth of the
child's rather than the child inertia alone. Implicit and explicit timesteps
differ to keep the explicit mass-extreme cases in their stable range.

### P5 GPU acceleration motors — initial implementation

The motor oracle now includes external body loads. CPU force-model velocity
drives incorporate those loads in their implicit feedback solve, while
acceleration-model drives retain their per-axis estimate. The analytic fixture
checks that distinction as well as floating-pair net momentum under external
loading. The expanded moderate-gain fixture covers 768 configurations; its CPU
run passes in `motor-model-loaded-cpu.log`.

The GPU Featherstone kernel now binds the existing `joint_motor_model` control
buffer and obtains effective inertia from unit articulated responses. It applies
explicit acceleration-scaled feedback or implicit mass-scaled feedback after
factorization, preserving physical motor caps and aggregate effort limits.
Effort mode remains unscaled. The later all-loads velocity solve excludes
acceleration-model rows, matching the CPU contract. Runtime guards still reject
brakes and unknown model values; low-level acceleration feedback requires
rigorous dynamics. No CPU fallback or new per-step mass readback is used.

## Remaining work / next implementation boundary

### General loop acceptance audit

The GPU test `tree_and_loop_joint_kinds_detach_at_the_same_support_load`
does not exercise every named kind as a loop: Fixed, Revolute, Prismatic, Ball
and D6 are tree cases; only Distance and rigid Ball are external cases.
At this historical pre-port checkpoint, `rigid_world_gpu::validate` still rejects other active loop kinds and compliant
Ball loops. The existing `insert_rigid_loop_joint` API itself accepts only Ball;
the general Fixed/Revolute/Prismatic/D6 loop API is `insert_loop_joint` with
explicit `JointSoftness`. Porting those existing compliant loops, rather than
substituting rigid links, is the missing path for broader P3 loop acceptance.

The CPU source supplies a concrete reference: `loop_forces::rows` uses joint
frame translation and quaternion-sign-canonical SO(3) logarithms, the angular
log Jacobian, locked/bounded axes and motor rows. `apply_selected` constructs
coupled articulated response, scales compliance by per-row effective mass,
adds `1 / (dt * (damping + dt * stiffness))` to its response diagonal, solves
bounded impulses and adds the resulting wrenches before the predictor.
For a translational closure row, both endpoint wrenches use the **child anchor**
as their application point (with opposite signs); the parent's lever arm is
not merely its authored parent-anchor arm. That detail preserves the rotating
parent-frame translation derivative and equal/opposite resultant torque.
It must not be lost by reusing radial endpoint Jacobians unchanged.

The retained GPU distance/cone path already groups connected articulations,
owns joint-to-row identities and assembles mass/Jacobian response. It currently
enumerates point constraints, cones and selected scalar tree bounds, not the
general compliant rows above. This audit identifies reuse candidates and the
ordering/frame requirements; it is not an implemented GPU loop path or a
decision to change the existing compliant physical law. Keep the capability
guard until the device solve, reaction/break readout and independent runtime
oracles exist.

## Key Learnings:

1. The initial GPU runtime bridge supplies device body velocities and substeps,
   but refreshed contacts and general constraint/reaction processing remain open.
2. Scalar equality locks require consistent subspace exclusion and zero-velocity
   integration on both backends; unilateral stop solving alone does not cover them.
3. Existing distance projections do not prove coupled endpoint response. Runtime
   CPU distance links now use shared anchor Jacobians and articulated impulses;
   GPU now implements the same radial contract, including selected sleeping islands
   and prescribed moving kinematic endpoints.
4. Loaded velocity-drive parity requires coupled predicted-velocity feedback;
   isolated motor damping stabilization is not equivalent under external loads.
5. A zero maximum is an anchor-coincidence constraint even without a minimum;
   a zero minimum alone must not constrain an arbitrary radial direction.
6. Redundant bilateral links require rank-aware load sharing, not just matching
   trajectories; GPU conjugate-gradient response now passes the per-link oracle.
7. Prepared CRBA/Jacobian bindings allow device-only substeps without recurring
   GPU buffer/bind-group construction, while retaining the legacy dispatch API.
8. Constraint redrift must respect the whole-articulation sleep mask, including
   latent non-waking rates; skipping forces alone does not preserve sleeping state.
9. GPU kinematic boundaries require prescribed anchor-velocity bias in radial rows
   and body-flag-aware Featherstone kinematics, not just a zero inverse mass.
10. A coincident positive radial bound needs an endpoint-antisymmetric limiting
    direction; a fixed +X normal violates exchange symmetry on both backends.
11. Implicit free-root COM coordinates eliminate the observed rotating-COM linear
    momentum drift; mass edits must reseed that frame while preserving physical
    state. General framed/articulated and angular-momentum gates remain distinct.
12. Non-cardinal f32 cone geometry near the antipode is sensitive to basis and
    derivative cancellation; canonical-basis requests and radial/azimuthal rows
    pass component parity but do not certify runtime impact dynamics.
13. Tree-cone relative joint coordinates eliminate the observed rotated zero-stop
    reaction error. Combining retained predictor increments and constraint
    impulses before the velocity update fixes the sampled diagonal loaded-twist
    regression without relaxing its gates; broader precision coverage remains.
14. Infinite plane endpoints are valid broadphase inputs even though their
    midpoint is NaN. Validate endpoints before filtering non-finite centroids.
15. A rigid external ball anchor can share the same three point-coincidence rows
    as a zero-radius constraint without modifying either endpoint tree. Keep its
    anchor-force samples separate from its cone-torque samples.
16. A zero-DOF joint can transmit a nonzero wrench even when its generalized
    effort vector is empty. Reconstruct the subtree wrench before projecting onto
    motion subspaces, and shift torque to the authored anchor explicitly.
17. Compiled scene identity is not solved-load validity: gravity and in-place,
    non-waking force/control edits require a separate dynamics-input stamp.
18. Zero prescribed COM acceleration does not mean zero spatial acceleration:
    a translating/rotating boundary requires `-omega cross v_COM` at a fixed
    recursion origin on both CPU and GPU.
19. Zero-length GPU DOF arrays have no uploaded buffer. Fixed-tree wrench dispatch
    needs retained dummy input bindings, not an invented free coordinate.
20. GPU vector normalization can lose very large finite loads through reciprocal
    underflow. Range-scale peak norms and reject overflow before publishing samples.
21. Broken edges must release authored topology as well as solver constraints;
    otherwise replacement edges fail even after physical detachment.
22. Joint-owned collision restrictions and explicit user pair exclusions need
    independent stable storage so breaking one cannot erase the other.
23. A broken joint changes dense DOF offsets mid-frame; accumulate diagnostic
    efforts by stable body/joint/local-DOF identity before mapping the final layout.
24. Solver rollback checkpoints need a separate input-edit guard: model identity
    alone cannot distinguish a restorable solver commit from a gravity/control edit.
25. GPU simultaneous break detection must finish in every workgroup before a
    separate ordered pass publishes the global halt flag.
26. Queued post-halt copies may preserve the correct boundary without a host poll
    per substep; redrift and all later sample writes must also respect the halt.
27. Tangential impulse coefficients must be combined independently; legacy scalar
    authoring maps to both, without repurposing viscous stiffness or smoothing.
28. Nearly redundant contact rows can stall block iterations despite small impulse
    updates. Validate velocity KKT residuals and use a coupled disk solve fallback.
29. Compliant normal redistribution causes a finite initial elastic displacement;
    measure both that displacement and sustained post-settling creep under load.
30. A no-readback API name is not evidence of residency: inspect every helper for
    mapping/polling and test multiple producer/refit/consumer sequences in one encoder.
31. Device broad-phase overflow must reach downstream fault handling even when
    the truncated candidate list contains few or no eligible exact contacts.
32. Retained narrow-phase faults must survive later zero-pair substeps; clear them
    only at an explicit boundary, and separately clear retired contact slots.
33. Conservative device bounds need padding based on uncancelled transform
    magnitudes, not just the resulting world center.
34. Cross-workgroup arrival counters do not publish non-atomic tree data safely;
    independent topology and ordered level refits remove that dependency.
35. Stable scene exclusions already compile to dense shape pairs; consume that
    table after topology changes instead of duplicating joint/body ownership policy.
36. Plane manifolds need per-pair point counts and endpoint witnesses; a single EPA
    result cannot represent the four separated corners of a resting box.
37. Check analytic contact locations as well as depth and normal: the prior
    capsule-plane midpoint had the wrong sign despite passing its old tests.
38. Nearly tied depths can reorder CPU/f64 versus GPU/f32 box contacts. Validate
    one-to-one geometric sets and independently enforce endpoint-exchange symmetry.
39. Disk rim samples do not guarantee grazing-plane detection. Evaluate radial
    extrema and bypass redundant-sample thresholds when every sample is separated.
40. A single cylinder support witness can jump between axial endpoints at a tie;
    separate disk supports preserve both the manifold span and endpoint parity.
41. Support direction magnitude must not select a different disk witness. Scale
    radial normalization and cone support comparisons before norms or dot products.
42. Keep persistent external wrenches separate from generated normal forces;
    otherwise a device substep chain can accumulate the previous contact load.
43. Contact incidence links can be published by atomic insertion and consumed in
    a later ordered pass; fixed slot indexing does not imply bitwise sum ordering.
44. Transporting both coefficients and conveyor velocity is not a friction solve;
    certify normal-force consumption separately from sustained tangential holding.
45. Disk convergence must evaluate the rounded published impulse; normalization
    and radius division can otherwise create or hide a velocity KKT violation.
46. A device-reported residual needs an independent higher-precision reconstruction;
    basis rotations and reciprocal scaling exposed f32 acceptance and compensated
    sum rounding issues. A smaller tolerance alone did not resolve them.
47. Coupled disk algebra and device residency do not establish live GPU friction;
    contact response assembly, impulse application and trajectories remain separate gates.
48. Deterministic contact indexing requires ordering after parallel grouping;
    an atomic append order is not a stable disk-solver row order.
49. Prepared device sorts need independent scratch and immutable uniforms when
    different lengths or repeated producers are queued in a single encoder.
50. A shared immovable boundary does not couple dynamic response groups, while
    a positive-load dynamic link can couple them even with zero tangential friction.
51. Per-island articulation CSR avoids scanning every scene articulation for each
    contact Gram block and preserves a deterministic summation/member order.
52. Input-pose COM Jacobians plus predicted generalized-rate increments reproduce
    the CPU friction predictor without discarding articulation cross-coupling.
53. A normalized disk iterate can stall after physical cap/scale rounding; evaluate
    and refine the actual published impulse without relaxing its velocity KKT gate.
54. Initial compliant support deflection and sustained tangential creep are different
    measurements; CPU/GPU agreement alone does not satisfy a holding bound.
55. A quotient-based radial-gap correction understated adjacent-float disk errors
    on the tested GPU. Compensated squared-radius differences pass direct f64 checks
    across boundary neighbors, angles and reciprocal scales.
56. A one-step static-to-dynamic timing difference can accumulate millimetres of
    trajectory error even when both per-step disk solves satisfy their KKT gates.
57. Predictor/redrift coordinate compensation must copy the input state's residues
    again for redrift; carrying provisional output residues double-counts motion.
58. A capture band used during compliant support redistribution cannot simply be
    replaced by the disk KKT tolerance; the stricter trial broke sustained holding.
59. Adding a stored coordinate residue to a much larger increment can erase it;
    retain both sum errors and renormalize after cancellation, not only after drift.
60. Preserving coordinate residues does not expose them to collision geometry;
    propagate translation residues through FK and consume them before rounding depth.
61. The TwoSum error itself needs an explicit GPU rounding boundary before it is
    combined with further low terms; otherwise the sampled relative-center sum lost
    those terms despite preserving the high sum and intermediate differences.
62. Speed-weighted disk complementarity can accept static creep near capacity;
    a curvature-scaled radial residual detects the sampled false-convergence window
    without changing the capture band or friction coefficients.
63. Retiring contact scratch after a sticky fault is insufficient for state safety;
    force/rate publication must consume the same status as prediction and redrift.
64. A live finite-ground fixture exposed shallow sphere-box EPA failure despite
    passing plane-contact trajectories; analytic closest features must preserve
    low translations before computing penetration, not only before integration.
65. Contact reaction reconstruction needs complete boundary COM loads and retained
    predictor-plus-tangent increments, not predictor forces or rounded rate differences.
66. Structural immobility is a body property within an articulation: a fixed
    ancestor remains an island boundary even when one of its descendants can move.
67. Diagnostic capture recompilation must preserve physical coordinate residues;
    otherwise toggling readout can change a small-motion trajectory.
68. A break segment's checkpoint is not the whole frame's checkpoint: rollback
    must retain the original model, solver and low-state buffers across rebuilds.
69. Newly enabled collision pairs need live geometric coverage; a sphere-sphere
    EPA failure appeared only after removing a joint's collision restriction.
70. Friction-mode promotion must wait for the global joint/contact KKT solution;
    a bilateral row can remove slip that an isolated contact would classify as sliding.
71. A zero-response scalar row can already satisfy complementarity while another
    block is still solving; a zero global Lipschitz constant is not alone a fault.
72. Contact-only island compaction omits zero-contact roots; unified response must
    explicitly retain joint-only islands rather than relying on dependency edges alone.
73. Scalar graph vertices retain constraints with no responsive endpoint while
    articulation CSR stays empty; inconsistent immovable rows can then fail explicitly.
74. Joint row export must exclude the predictor increment when common response
    assembly will add it; otherwise mixed rows count the same physical acceleration twice.
75. Shared scalar multipliers need their original row direction and kind to preserve
    joint force/torque averaging and active-bound tags in runtime readouts.
76. Joint-row reservations must not enlarge the public contact capacity; count
    normal rows separately from the combined scalar/contact island width.
77. Final sticking does not necessarily imply a static cap: a joint may remove
    initial contact slip while the shared solve still uses the dynamic coefficient.
78. Compensated drift requires scalar stop gaps to consume the same coordinate
    residues; rounded coordinates alone caused measurable bound-edit stop jitter.
79. A sleeping-island runtime hook can bypass the ordinary step hook; both must
    defer and consume the common constraint stage with the same selected bodies.
80. Redundant contact/joint rows can satisfy the same KKT and motion gates with
    different joint multipliers, so per-joint reaction and break parity need an
    explicit allocation policy rather than looser velocity tolerances.
81. Minimum-norm allocation must preserve both the Gram response and the linear
    objective; preserving velocity alone can move to a different primary objective.
82. GPU orthogonal projections must use the norm of the stored basis vector;
    assuming an exactly unit f32 vector produced secondary convergence stalls.
83. Strictly inactive scalar impulses must stay exactly zero, and affine-tangent
    disks need facial reduction; otherwise valid primary solutions can fail in
    a secondary allocation stage.
84. Prescribed world COM/angular derivatives require an angular-acceleration
    reference-point shift in spatial recursion, not just a linear acceleration bias.
85. An instantaneous inverse-dynamics acceleration input does not define kinematic
    runtime motion; prediction, drift, relative constraint bias and break sampling
    still need a consistent per-substep boundary-motion contract.
86. Prescribed acceleration changes the free constraint-row velocity even though
    it is not a generalized DOF increment; propagate that bias through dynamic
    descendants without changing the input-slip friction classification.
87. Advancing an offset-COM kinematic body requires COM integration followed by
    reconstruction of the body origin; predictor/redrift must reuse input state
    rather than advance the prescribed motion twice.
88. Packed GPU contact rows contain both collider and body IDs. Boundary motion
    must use the body fields; inherited-support fixtures expose the distinction
    when an unshaped kinematic ancestor shifts body indices away from collider IDs.
89. An accelerating-from-rest capture fixture must demand more than the dynamic
    friction capacity but less than the static capacity to independently detect
    accidental classification from predicted slip instead of input slip.
90. Translation compensation cannot depend on a nonempty generalized-coordinate
    buffer: an isolated driven root can have zero coordinates and still accumulate
    physically meaningful displacement below an f32 ULP.
91. Preserving low state only in contact scenes makes collider presence change
    small-motion integration. Contact-free stepping needs the same frame, rebuild
    and break-rollback precision lifecycle as the contact path.
92. Numeric handles can coincide across independent scenes and divergent forks;
    precision caches need insertion identity as well as stable handle and layout
    compatibility before transferring retained state.
93. A rejected frame after an explicit pose edit must restore the edited input's
    precision checkpoint, not reset unrelated bodies or restore pre-edit geometry.
94. The CPU rigid penalty path ignores restitution too; an elastic spring bounce
    independent of the authored coefficient is not a valid GPU parity oracle.
95. Impact friction capacity must include the solved normal impact impulse, not
    just the normal penalty predictor's impulse.
96. Newton normal restitution and post-impact Coulomb complementarity can satisfy
    their equations while increasing oblique-impact energy; normal rebound tests
    alone do not certify the production restitution law.
97. Midpoint impact friction pairs impulses with average velocity; a zero average
    slip can mean reversal, not final sticking at rest.
98. Solving a coupled contact as separate normal and tangent iterations can fail
    at high friction even for a positive-definite response; a complete local
    three-row solve resolves the measured case without weakening its gates.
99. A dynamic descendant's physical kinetic energy includes inherited kinematic
    motion; impact boundary-work accounting needs projected body momentum, not
    just reduced joint rates.
100. A positive-definite tensor is not sufficient for a physical rigid inertia:
     its principal moments must also satisfy the triangle inequalities.
101. A permanent onset penetration offset changes loaded equilibrium height;
     restitution correction must not redefine the penalty spring's rest depth.
102. Impact activation belongs to connected dynamic groups; sharing fixed ground
     must not change an unrelated contact trajectory.
103. Nearly dependent manifold rows need inactive-impulse release, including in
     the position stage; contact-only fallback does not repair scalar correction.
104. A fixed-radius tangent disk solver is not an impact solver: the normal impulse
     and its friction radius must be solved together, alongside scalar joint rows.
105. Singular tangent response needs explicit range/null-direction handling;
     determinant inversion and huge failure-sentinel norms are unsafe in that path.
106. Impact island activation cannot use penalty force or friction as its gate;
     frictionless contacts with zero onset penalty still need normal impulse rows.
107. Writing acceleration storage alone does not activate prescribed boundary
     motion; use the authored setter so the driven flag and data agree.
108. Episode history must key collider insertion identity, not compacted shape IDs
     or contact row order; separate compiled pieces of one collider share a token.
109. Onset selection must follow complete dynamic contact/joint unions, before
     packed-capacity checks; unselected groups must not consume impact capacity.
110. Zeroing onset force or persistent restitution can hide invalid source values;
     validate those fields before modifying the row.
111. Separating contacts can still connect an impact group; filter their solver
     rows only after forming the full dynamic contact/joint graph.
112. Cache the predicted normal speed used for inclusion and reuse it in assembly
     so rounding cannot change the sign between selection and impact validation.
113. Export geometric position gaps directly; subtracting a large velocity from a
     velocity residual can erase a small gap before position correction begins.
114. A zero-depth onset can still select joint position constraints even though it
     contributes no contact displacement row; velocity and position selection differ.
115. Generalized position displacement has no velocity units; applying physical
     velocity caps to it can leave an onset gap unresolved even after a valid solve.
116. Prediction, position application and redrift need six retained binding sets
     for two ping-pong states plus a projected state, not the previous two slots.
117. Response-only kinematic fixtures can omit a tree joint, but GPU integration
     requires an articulated driven body; the application fixture must include it.
118. A partitioned friction stage must carry impact-corrected rates through excluded
     groups instead of reconstructing those rates from the original predictor.
119. Merge physical responses by active row ownership, not nonzero impulse alone;
     an active zero-impulse scalar still has a valid regime and diagnostic record.
120. Reaction reconstruction must add the predictor increment once to the combined
     impact/friction increment and must never consume position-displacement output.
121. Automatic joint detachment changes structural stamps without creating a new
     contact episode; preserving existing pair history prevents a false second
     impact and projection, including when restitution is zero.
122. A f32 impulse can have no representable neighbour with a smaller residual even
     above a fixed absolute tolerance; test representability and report raw residuals.
123. Sphere-box contact points must use the midpoint of both surface witnesses;
     a wrong half-depth sign changes friction torque even when normals and depths agree.
124. Episode rollback must restore host identity tokens as well as device history;
     restoring the last published physical input must not create a new impact solely
     because edit stamps changed during a failed attempt.
125. Dropping a zero-depth sphere-box row changes impact episode lifetime; preserving
     a touching episode and applying a penalty force are separate decisions. Check
     loaded settling as well as short impact and break-event parity.
126. Whole-loop GPU timestamps include host/queue idle; post-frame allocation samples
     are not transient peaks, and state-transfer counters are not total traffic.
     Benchmark output must name these scopes instead of inventing complete metrics.
127. Feature-gated benchmarks need an explicit feature-enabled check; workspace
     all-target checks can legitimately skip targets whose required features are off.
128. Count actual command-encoding sites, not an estimated stage multiplier; halted
     substeps and model recompilation can encode work that does not execute shader
     bodies. Thread-local scopes also prevent unrelated worker counts leaking in.
129. A zero HAL allocation counter with nonzero buffer memory is unavailable data,
     not evidence of zero allocations. Keep live-buffer and transient-peak metrics distinct.
130. Multi-DOF drive support needs real position coordinates in both ordinary and
     stabilized assembly; removing a host rejection alone does not certify it.
131. XYZ limit projection must recompose in the same product order it decomposes;
     a single-axis fixture with zero other angles cannot detect reversed products.
132. Detect Euler singularity using the cosine magnitude, not a loose threshold
     on sine near one; premature collapse changes otherwise resolvable coordinates.
133. A GPU worker can remain alive in an indefinite poll after a driver context
     timeout. Preserve device/kernel evidence and distinguish process supervision
     from a physics or driver fix; a quiet log alone proves neither completion nor failure.
134. A contact-count assertion can mistake self-contact for floor coverage. Check
     endpoint identity and preload; preserve physically valid stiction cases when
     repairing a controller fixture whose convergence expectation ignored friction.
135. Size per-invocation articulated scratch by maximum articulation width, not
     scene count; keep joint and feedback-row bounds separate.
136. Successful device fences do not prove solver success. Read the fault word
     and numerical outputs, and reproduce control/threshold uploads in diagnostics.
137. World-origin spatial inertia can lose unit-scale rotational inertia in f32
     at large translations. Shift all spatial columns, loads and prescribed
     kinematics consistently to an articulation-local reference; keep world
     publication separate and verify unchanged physical response.
138. Forward dynamics and reaction reconstruction must consume the same control
     body wrench exactly once; subtracting an unapplied control fabricates reactions.
139. Scanning all authored joints inside every articulation's reaction pass gives
     quadratic owner lookup for independent bodies. Group by CSR range once and
     preserve authored order and stable-handle mapping through compaction.
140. Cargo test and Cargo bench need distinct defaults for custom harnesses;
     verify parent and worker mode labels without treating smoke execution as
     the required performance matrix.
141. A running aggregate can execute binaries compiled before new tests existed;
     inspect the executed target and test list before applying its result to
     the current source tree.
142. A single endpoint contact cannot represent a parallel capsule support span;
     retaining bounded endpoint contacts repairs the measured XPBD stack without
     changing its fixture or weakening acceptance.
143. Momentum-conserving coordinate integration and reaction reconstruction share
     rate-frame conventions. A published-rate correction alone can fabricate
     reaction loads or feed the wrong rate representation into redrift.
144. Advancing world momentum without advancing the articulation centroid can
     conserve angular momentum about a fixed origin while still drifting the
     intrinsic angular momentum about the moving COM.
145. Centroid transport must retain an impact's geometric position reference;
     restarting from the pre-projection pose can erase penetration correction
     and cause a second impulse, rebound or energy gain.
146. `needs_drop` does not measure heap allocation: inline descriptors can retain
     reference-counted device/lease handles without allocating during construction.
     Measure allocation directly and test layout separately.
147. Positive Cholesky pivots alone do not certify full rank for a rotated
     near-singular matrix; bound inverse-factor norms or use the spectral fallback.
148. Accumulate centroids relative to one body COM so coincident point masses do
     not acquire artificial parallel-axis inertia from multiply/divide roundoff.
149. Runtime compilation already provides a validated spectral `body_inv_inertia`;
     GPU isolated-root dynamics can consume it without reconstructing rank in f32.
150. Very weak rotational modes expose cancellation in world-spatial translational
     bias; compute isolated-body acceleration about COM before mapping to joint rates.
151. A sub-ULP radial gap can reverse a reported force after timestep scaling;
     preserve the authored bound residue and compensate the squared-distance difference.
152. Acceleration-drive scaling uses the inverse articulated mass diagonal, not
     child mass alone; floating pairs provide an independent reduced-inertia oracle.
153. Preserving a constraint bound's low bits is insufficient if anchor evaluation
     discards position residues; retain and renormalize both sides of the gap.
154. Retained arithmetic cannot recover authored low bits discarded at upload;
     seed precision buffers from f64 inputs initially and on edited/new entries.
155. CPU acceleration velocity drives use the per-axis effective-inertia estimate
     but skip the later force-drive all-loads solve; GPU parity must preserve that
     distinction, which no-load scalar fixtures cannot detect.
156. Applying huge explicit motor forces and subtracting them for implicit feedback
     can erase the physical acceleration in f32; apply deferred feedback directly.
157. Forward dynamics and inverse reactions must use the same quaternion rotation
     convention: normalization roundoff can otherwise create false reaction loads
     when a small motor wrench is recovered beside a large external wrench.
158. A finite zero inverse-mass diagonal denotes a null response, not a numerical
     fault; skip that motor correction without disabling supported drive axes.
159. Single-axis normalized Euler quaternion integration advances angle by
     `2*atan(omega*dt/2)`; an independent discrete oracle must distinguish this
     from exponential rotation by `omega*dt` without weakening its tolerance.
160. Compensating squared radial gaps is not enough for exact representable
     outputs: preserve the denominator sum residue and correct quotient rounding
     with the numerator's retained tail and an FMA residual.
161. Recomputing a predicted rate can round differently under FMA and falsely
     classify unconstrained integration as a velocity override; retain the actual
     pre-limit rate when deciding whether to publish the analytical increment.
162. Coplanar contact Gram matrices are rank deficient. Pivoted residual validation
     avoids magnifying their rounding tails through artificial positive null pivots;
     keep validation separate from the physical Gram matrix and friction law.
